lead.title: A third of family offices expect a change of leader within five years, and the house they run is being professionalised along with the portfolio
lead.standfirst: Citi Wealth's 2026 Global Family Office Report, published yesterday, finds families confident about returns but newly urgent about succession, cross border complexity and the way their own offices are run.
lead.body:
Citi Wealth published its 2026 Global Family Office Report on Tuesday 22 September. It is compiled by the bank's Global Family Office Group, which works with more than 1,900 family offices worldwide, and it rests on a survey of 351 offices in 41 countries conducted in June and July. The survey was launched at Citi's eleventh Family Office Leadership Summit in June, attended by more than 150 family office leaders from over 25 countries with an average family net worth of USD 2.1 billion. This is the upper tier of private wealth, the families whose houses, aircraft and staff are run as organisations in their own right.

The headline numbers are calm. Nearly 90 per cent of respondents reported positive portfolio performance for the year to date, and 41 per cent continue to target annual returns of between 7 and 10 per cent. Geopolitical shocks tested portfolios without triggering retreat: more than 40 per cent made no major changes at all. Inflation has replaced trade disputes and tariffs as the leading worry, followed by interest rates, the stability of the financial system and market volatility. Public equities have returned as the first destination for new money, with nearly half of offices increasing their exposure, while private markets remain a pillar of the portfolio.

The more revealing findings concern the family rather than the market. Roughly one third of respondents expect a leadership transition in the family, the family office or the family business within the next five years. They name unclear succession plans, insufficiently prepared heirs and a lack of agreement on the family's future as their main obstacles. Families are answering with education programmes, seats for the next generation in governance and hands on learning. At the same time, 38 per cent expect the family itself to become more international over the next five years, with assets, businesses and members spread across several jurisdictions, and tax coordination, structuring and compliance growing accordingly.

Citi describes a broader shift it calls professionalisation beyond investing. Offices are applying institutional discipline to operations, risk, succession and organisational development, and artificial intelligence is moving from experiment to daily use in reporting, information management and workflow, with productivity rather than investment returns as the goal and final decisions left to experienced people. The report organises its conclusions around three words: capital, capability and continuity.
lead.why: When a family office professionalises and prepares a new generation, the household side follows: clearer reporting lines, written procedures, and principals who may change within a few years. The estate manager who can document how a house runs, and brief an heir as well as a founder, becomes part of the continuity plan.

articles.title: Seattle has voted to require a written agreement for every household job, and the family that employs will need records to prove it
articles.body:
On 15 September, Seattle City Council approved council bill 121266, amending the city's Domestic Workers Ordinance. The amended law takes effect on 1 July 2027, the same day as Washington's new statewide protections for domestic workers, which the city's Office of Labor Standards says it was designed to align with. Seattle passed the first municipal domestic workers bill of rights in the United States in 2018, in force since 2019; the office notes that a dozen other jurisdictions have since followed, with Washington the thirteenth state to legislate.

The amendments proposed in August and now adopted change the paperwork of private service. They require a written agreement between the hiring household and the domestic worker. They require the household to create and retain records of pay and hours. They add protection against retaliation for workers who take paid sick and safe leave or other agreed time off. They require advance notice before a job is ended, and they bring enforcement into line with the city's other labour standards.

The existing floor remains in place. Domestic workers in Seattle are entitled to the city minimum wage, USD 21.30 an hour in 2026, a 30 minute uninterrupted meal period after five consecutive hours, and a paid 10 minute rest break for every four hours, with extra pay where the work makes a break impossible. Live in staff are entitled to an unpaid 24 hour rest period if asked to work more than six days in a row. Households may not hold a worker's passport or other original documents. The ordinance covers childcare, housekeeping, cooking, gardening and home management, and applies to employees and independent contractors alike.

The practical consequence is that the informal arrangement, a verbal agreement and a monthly transfer, will no longer satisfy the law in the city. Offer letters, schedules, time records and termination notices become documents a household must be able to produce.
articles.why: In a staffed house it is usually the estate or house manager who holds the contracts, the timesheets and the leave calendar. Rules like Seattle's turn that administrative work into legal protection for the family, and into a core competence for whoever runs the team.

articles.title: Prime London is selling again, but only to buyers who mean to live there, and the house that sits on the market loses a fifth of its price
articles.body:
After a decade that began with the Brexit referendum and ended with the abolition of the non dom regime, London's prime market is showing movement. Knight Frank recorded a 14 per cent rise in the number of prime deals in the three months to July compared with the same period of 2025, with Prime Central London up 3 per cent. Its August figures show transactions across prime central and prime outer London running 2 per cent above the five year average, and prime central sales 6 per cent higher than a year earlier.

Prices have not followed. Average values in Prime Central London fell 3.3 per cent in the year to August and are 23 per cent lower over eleven years, according to Knight Frank. Savills puts the fall from the 2014 peak at 26.3 per cent. LonRes reports an annual decline of almost 8 per cent in achieved prices, with more than half of the homes sold in July having been reduced at least once and an average discount of 10.4 per cent off the original asking price. Time on the market is the tell: homes sold within three months this year went for less than 4 per cent below asking, while those that took a year or more sold at a discount of more than 19 per cent.

The buying agency Black Brick describes a market cleared of speculators. Its buyers are split fairly evenly between British families buying a main home and international clients either relocating or looking for a pied a terre. One of its recent acquisitions illustrates the second group: a North American family bought an apartment of more than 3,000 square feet at The Whiteley in Bayswater, the conversion of London's first department store, turnkey, with furnishings and artwork included, choosing it for security and residents' services including a pool, spa, private members' club and a Six Senses hotel.

Knight Frank's head of prime central London sales says buyers are now using pre Budget speculation and bond market nervousness to negotiate the price down rather than walk away. The Budget is due on 28 October.
articles.why: A market of end users means more families actually moving in, often into serviced buildings where the household team must work alongside a concierge, a spa and building security. Knowing how a turnkey purchase, furniture and art included, is inventoried and handed over is part of the arrival.

articles.title: The largest managed fleet of private jets in the world is due to be formed this month, and the family aircraft may change hands without changing owner
articles.body:
Solairus Aviation, based in Petaluma, California, agreed on 7 August to acquire the aircraft management and charter divisions of Clay Lacy Aviation, the Los Angeles operator founded in 1968. Solairus manages about 360 aircraft from more than 100 bases across North America and employs more than 1,200 flight crew and support staff. Clay Lacy manages about 140. Once the deal completes, Solairus will operate what it describes as the world's largest managed fleet, more than 500 aircraft. Closing is targeted for the end of September, subject to regulatory approvals, and financial terms have not been disclosed.

Aircraft management is the quiet layer beneath private flying. The owner holds the jet; the management company hires and trains the pilots and cabin crew, arranges maintenance, handles insurance and regulatory compliance, and may charter the aircraft to others when the family is not using it, offsetting its cost. Both companies argue that scale now matters: greater size, they say, helps absorb rising costs, negotiate better prices and widen access while keeping personal service. By early September, more than 80 per cent of Clay Lacy's aircraft owners had committed to move with the business, according to Private Jet Card Comparisons.

Clay Lacy does not disappear. Its FBO terminals at Van Nuys and John Wayne Airport in California and at Waterbury Oxford in Connecticut, its maintenance centres and its aviation real estate stay under the Clay Lacy name and current ownership, with a further FBO planned to serve Sun Valley, Idaho. The company's chairman describes the future Clay Lacy as an aviation infrastructure platform built around those businesses.

The consolidation follows a crowded month in American business aviation, in which the charter broker ONEflight paused its sales activity, and it lands in a market where owners are weighing reliability of service against the personal relationships that bound them to smaller operators.
articles.why: For the family office or house manager who coordinates travel, a change of management company means new contacts, new trip request procedures and possibly new crew. Knowing who actually operates the family aircraft, and who to call at 2 a.m., is part of the brief.

articles.title: A white gold Cartier made for a single collector has become the most valuable Cartier, and the most valuable quartz watch, ever sold at auction
articles.body: At Sotheby's Important Watches sale in Hong Kong last week, a unique white gold Cartier Cheich sold for HK$26.5 million with fees, about USD 3.38 million. It is now the most expensive Cartier wristwatch ever sold publicly and, because it runs on a battery, the most expensive quartz watch as well. The pre sale estimate was unusually wide, from HK$8 million to HK$40 million. The Cheich has one of the stranger origins in modern watchmaking. It was created as a prize for winners of the Paris Dakar rally in the years Cartier sponsored the race, and its case is modelled on the rally's emblem, the stylised head of a Tuareg man wearing a headscarf; cheich is the French rendering of sheikh. Four were made in yellow gold, and among the recipients were Thierry Sabine, founder of the rally, and Gaston Rahier, winner in 1984 and 1985. Sponsorship ended after Sabine's death in 1986. Rahier's example sold at Sotheby's in 2022 for a little over EUR 1 million. The watch sold last week is the only one in white gold, made roughly 25 years after the originals for Giorgio Seragnoli, a Bologna collector who once owned the world's largest collection of Cartier watches before his fortune was spent. It passed through an Italian dealer to the consignor. The buyer was anonymous. According to SJX Watches, the result confirms continuing demand for Cartier's shaped watches, the category that includes the Crash, and the same sale set a new benchmark for a rare Cartier London Midi Pebble. The lesson for anyone valuing a collection is that the movement inside no longer decides the price. Rarity, provenance and the story of who commissioned a piece now carry more weight than mechanical complication.
articles.why: Watches are among the most portable and most frequently misplaced valuables in a household. A collection register with photographs, serial numbers, provenance papers and insurance values is the standard, and a piece like this shows why its paperwork can be worth as much as its case.

briefs.b: Flexjet opened a USD 34 million, 2,098 square metre private terminal at Farnborough Airport on 10 September, its first in Europe, reserved for its own owners and guests with dedicated security screening and immigration. The building also houses an expanded Red Label Academy, a finishing school style training centre for the company's nearly 300 cabin servers. Flexjet now has nine terminals open or in development in the United States, including Teterboro.

The number of British residential mortgages of GBP 5 million or more rose to 333 last year from 313, worth GBP 3.3 billion in total with an average loan of about GBP 10 million, according to Karis Capital. Some 88 per cent were secured on London properties. Wealthy buyers who could pay cash are increasingly borrowing to keep capital invested elsewhere.

To implement the High Value Council Tax Surcharge on English homes worth GBP 2 million or more, officials from HMRC's Valuation Office will carry out the first national valuation exercise since 1991, visiting homes in person, with fines of up to GBP 200 for owners who refuse entry. Annual charges run from GBP 2,500 to GBP 7,500 from April 2028. Residents of Kensington and Chelsea, Wandsworth, Richmond and Westminster are expected to pay about half the total.

lead.title: A fortune held in code now belongs to 135,694 people, and the households it is starting to build run on different assumptions
lead.standfirst: Henley & Partners counts 290 crypto centi millionaires and 23 crypto billionaires, a cohort that is younger, more mobile and more secretive than the wealth private service was built around.
lead.body:
The Crypto Wealth Report 2026, published by Henley & Partners on 8 September, puts 135,694 individuals in possession of at least USD 1 million in digital assets. Of those, 92,272 hold that million in Bitcoin alone. Above them sit 290 centi millionaires with USD 100 million or more, 151 of them in Bitcoin, and 23 billionaires, of whom nine are Bitcoin billionaires. The total market stood at USD 2.6 trillion as at 31 August 2026, USD 1.6 trillion of it in Bitcoin.

The striking figure is the base beneath the pyramid. Some 742 million people now hold digital assets in some quantity, 371 million of them holding Bitcoin, and that number kept widening through a year in which the market itself contracted from its record highs. Singapore tops the report's Crypto Adoption Index for the fourth consecutive year, which matters less as a league table than as a signal of where this cohort chooses to keep a residence, a company and a banking relationship.

This is a small population by the standards of the wealth reports this Journal usually reads. Altrata counts more than half a million ultra wealthy individuals worldwide. A hundred and thirty five thousand crypto millionaires is a fraction of that, and a fortune in digital assets is rarely the whole of anyone's balance sheet. What makes the cohort worth understanding is its shape rather than its size. It skews young, it is unusually mobile, it is concentrated in a handful of jurisdictions, and it has been formed by an asset class where the loss of a credential is the loss of the asset itself.

That last point is the one that reaches the house. In a family whose wealth sits in property, art and securities, the custodians are banks, registrars and insurers, and a mistake by a member of staff is embarrassing rather than terminal. In a household where a material part of the fortune is a private key, the perimeter includes the study, the safe, the devices left charging in a kitchen and the person who answers the door to the engineer who has come to look at the network. The principal may be thirty two. The standards will be no softer for it.
lead.why: A new cohort of principals is forming, and it is young, mobile and unusually exposed to failures of physical and digital security. Household staff who understand device discipline, visitor control and the handling of anything that looks like a credential will be valuable to them in a way that polish alone is not.

articles.title: Confidentiality has become a line in the salary, and in Los Angeles it is written into three quarters of assistant contracts
articles.body:
Morgan & Mallet International's Household Staff Annual Report 2025/26, drawn from a database of more than 50,300 candidates and covering 28 positions across eight markets, states the matter plainly. Privacy adds 15 to 20 per cent to a salary. Candidates who can demonstrate discretion, rather than merely promise it, are placed at 10 to 15 per cent above market rates for the same role.

The clearest evidence sits in Los Angeles, where 77 per cent of personal assistant placements now require a signed non disclosure agreement. The agreement is not the point. What the figure describes is a market in which a household's exposure is assumed rather than argued about, and in which the assistant is treated as part of the family's risk management rather than as its diary keeper. In Miami, 79 per cent of placed assistants have already worked alongside a security team. In Manhattan, 91 per cent handle private school applications, a file that contains almost everything a family would least like to see circulated.

The money follows. American personal assistants are placed from USD 80,000 to USD 250,000, and executive assistants from USD 120,000 to USD 250,000, the widest band of any role in the report outside the chief of staff. The spread is not explained by typing speed. It is explained by what a family is prepared to hand over, and to whom.

Retention tells the same story from the other side. Ninety two per cent of assistants placed in Los Angeles stay two years or longer, in a sector where average tenure across all roles has collapsed to roughly three years. Eighty four per cent have worked for families worth USD 30 million or more. Households that have found someone they trust are visibly unwilling to repeat the exercise, and they pay to avoid it.

For a candidate entering the profession, this is the most actionable finding in the report. Language, cuisine and service technique can be taught in months. A verifiable record of confidentiality takes years and cannot be bought, which is exactly why it commands a premium that no qualification does.
articles.why: Discretion is the one part of the craft that is both priced explicitly and impossible to acquire quickly. A candidate who can point to years of confidential work, and to referees willing to confirm it, is negotiating from a different position than one who cannot.
articles.src: Morgan & Mallet International, Household Staff Annual Report 2025/26

articles.title: The supply of twin engine helicopters has fallen by a third in six months, and the family that wants one will be waiting
articles.body:
AeroAsset's twin engine helicopter report for the first half of 2026 records retail transactions up 8 per cent year on year while the number of aircraft available for sale fell 33 per cent. Sixty seven machines changed hands against only 123 left on the global market. The absorption rate has tightened to roughly 11 months, which is to say that at the current pace the entire world inventory of second hand twins would clear before next August.

The squeeze is not evenly spread. Light twins saw volume slip 4 per cent while inventory fell 44 per cent. Medium twins posted the strongest growth of any high volume category at 38 per cent, and their supply is now at a five year low. Heavy twins sold two more units than last year on supply down 10 per cent. North America accounted for 46 per cent of transactions and Europe for 31 per cent, with European volumes up 75 per cent year on year, while Asia Pacific fell 42 per cent and Latin America 47 per cent.

Liquidity, in this market, is a practical matter rather than an abstraction. The Airbus H135 and H145 families trade most readily, followed by the Leonardo AW109S and SP, the Bell 429 and the Sikorsky S-76C+ and C++. The Airbus H155 and the Sikorsky S-76D are the hardest to move. A family asking to buy the machine it already likes may find the answer is a two year wait or a different type.

None of this is remote from the house. The twin engine helicopter is the aircraft that connects an estate to an airport, a Mediterranean villa to a marina and a Swiss chalet to a valley floor in February. It is flown with two engines precisely because it carries principals over water and over cities. When the supply of those machines halves, the schedule that depends on them becomes less forgiving, charter rates firm, and the person building the family's diary has less margin for error than the year before.
articles.why: Estate and house managers increasingly coordinate rotary transfers as a matter of routine. A tightening market means fewer aircraft available at short notice, firmer charter pricing and longer lead times, all of which land on whoever holds the schedule.

articles.title: Seventeen of the twenty five most expensive wines in the world now come from two Burgundy domaines held by the same owner
articles.body:
WineCap's ranking of the most expensive fine wine brands of 2026, reported at the start of September, places Domaine de la Romanee-Conti at the summit at GBP 195,406 a case. Immediately behind it sits d'Auvenay's Chevalier-Montrachet Grand Cru at GBP 186,419 a case of twelve. What the list reveals, however, is concentration rather than hierarchy. Of the twenty five names, seventeen belong to just two houses, Domaine Leroy with eleven entries and Domaine d'Auvenay with six.

Both are the property of Lalou Bize-Leroy, who also retains a quarter share of Domaine de la Romanee-Conti. Together the two domaines account for 64.1 per cent of the ranking's combined value. The explanation is scarcity carried to an extreme. D'Auvenay farms 3.87 hectares spread across sixteen appellations, and its holding in Criots-Batard-Montrachet extends to 0.064 hectares, a parcel that yields a few hundred bottles in a good year.

White Burgundy is disproportionately represented at the very top, taking three of the four most expensive wines and five of the top ten, with an average case price of GBP 102,197 against GBP 74,822 for red. Only one wine in the top twenty five comes from outside Burgundy at all: Chave's Ermitage Cathelin, in fifteenth place at GBP 61,143. Screaming Eagle Sauvignon Blanc follows in twenty eighth, Petrus is the highest Bordeaux at forty sixth, Krug Clos du Mesnil the highest Champagne at eightieth and Soldera Case Basse the highest Italian at ninety ninth.

Prices at this altitude are not rising. Seventeen of the top twenty five declined by an average of 2.0 per cent over the last twelve months, and Romanee-Conti, for all its position, delivered the weakest ten year appreciation in the group at 70.9 per cent. The market has corrected since its 2022 peak and these bottles corrected with it.

For a household, the practical reading is about custody rather than investment. A cellar that contains any of these names holds objects whose value rests on provenance, condition and an unbroken record of storage. A single warm summer in a badly regulated room, or a case moved between houses without documentation, erases more value than most people imagine is at stake in a wine rack.
articles.why: Cellar management is a standard part of a senior household brief. Knowing which names carry this kind of value, and that their worth depends on temperature records and provenance rather than labels alone, is the difference between storing wine and looking after an asset.
articles.src: WineCap, reported by The Drinks Business

briefs.b: GlobalAir.com's marketplace snapshot of 1 September 2026 shows large cabin jets clearing fastest of any turbine class, at a median 79 days on the market against 6.5 months of supply. Midsize jets sit 131 days on 8.0 months, and twin turboprops 159 days. AMSTAT reports median heavy jet transaction values up 13 per cent year on year with only 5.2 per cent of that fleet listed for sale.

Frieze London and Frieze Masters return to The Regent's Park from 14 to 18 October. The invitation only preview falls on Wednesday 14 October, with general admission from the 15th. Tickets are date and time specific and sold online only, with no admission at the gate, so a principal's attendance has to be arranged well in advance.

Twenty two per cent of clients ask specifically for a traditional English butler holding certification from a recognised school, according to Morgan & Mallet. Butlers make up about 5 per cent of the agency's registered profiles, average seven years of experience and are placed at a 96 per cent success rate. Nine per cent of butlers worldwide are women. The highest placed salary, in the United States, reaches USD 180,000.

lead.title: Switzerland taxes a wealthy foreigner on the cost of her life, and the rent on the house sets the floor beneath the bill
lead.standfirst: Expenditure based taxation, the arrangement that has drawn internationally mobile families to Vaud, Valais and Ticino for a century, now carries a federal minimum base of CHF 434,700 and a rule that ties the whole calculation to the household's rent.
lead.body: Switzerland does not offer a flat tax. What it offers, to foreign nationals who take up residence and do not work here, is a different question entirely: rather than declaring worldwide income and assets, the taxpayer agrees a deemed base with the canton, and ordinary Swiss rates are then applied to that figure. The Federal Department of Finance calls it expenditure based taxation. Everyone else calls it the forfait. It remains one of the quietest and most consequential arrangements in European private wealth, and it is enjoying a second life now that the United Kingdom has closed its own regime for non domiciled residents. The mechanics are unusually concrete. The taxable base is the taxpayer's annual worldwide cost of living, but it may not fall below two floors. At federal level the minimum base is currently CHF 434,700. Separately, the base must be at least seven times the annual rent paid, or the rental value, of the principal residence in Switzerland. Cantons set their own minimum thresholds on top of that, and the final figure is confirmed by an individual ruling from the cantonal tax authority. A control calculation runs each year to ensure the agreed base never produces less tax than ordinary rates would on Swiss source income and on foreign income for which treaty relief is claimed. Cantonal wealth tax still applies, assessed on a minimum wealth base that is usually a multiple of the deemed income. The conditions are strict and they are personal. The taxpayer must not hold Swiss citizenship, must be taking up Swiss residence for the first time or after at least ten years away, and must not carry on any gainful activity in Switzerland. Employment abroad is generally fine, as is managing one's own assets. For married couples both spouses must satisfy every condition independently. The right ends the moment the person naturalises or takes a job here. The regime is also far smaller than its reputation suggests: fewer than 0.1 per cent of Swiss taxpayers use it, and at the end of 2018 the federal government counted 4,557 people paying a combined CHF 821 million in tax. Geography matters as much as arithmetic. Zurich abolished the cantonal regime after a popular vote in 2009, effective from January 2010, and Schaffhausen, Appenzell Ausserrhoden, Basel Landschaft and Basel Stadt followed. Federal lump sum taxation technically survives in those cantons, but with full cantonal and communal taxation on worldwide income it is of no practical use, which is why arrivals cluster in Vaud, Valais, Ticino and central Switzerland. Immigration runs on a separate track. Non EU nationals over 55 must show close personal ties to Switzerland; those under 55 are admitted on preponderant cantonal fiscal interest, which in practice means an annual tax contribution of roughly CHF 200,000 or more. Lump sum taxpayers also pay Swiss social security of around CHF 26,500 a year until the retirement age of 65.
lead.why: The seven times rent rule places the household's lease at the centre of the family's tax file. Whoever negotiates the tenancy, the rental value and the running costs of the house is contributing, directly, to a number the principal's advisers will defend to a cantonal authority.

articles.title: A Swiss household cannot simply hire from outside Europe, and the one door that opens needs two years of documented service
articles.body: For candidates holding an EU or EFTA passport, working in a Swiss private household is largely an administrative exercise. No visa or prior authorisation is required to enter. Engagements of up to 90 working days in a calendar year need only an online notification, filed by the employer before the first day of work. Beyond 90 days the worker registers at the commune within 14 days of arrival and before starting, and receives an EU/EFTA L permit for contracts up to a year or a B permit for longer or open ended roles. There are no quotas and no labour market test. After five years of continuous compliant residence a B permit holder may become eligible for a C permit. Occupational mobility is full: employers, roles and cantons can be changed without fresh authorisation. For everyone else the position is close to closed. Swiss work permits for third country nationals are reserved for highly skilled specialists who satisfy strict economic interest and labour market criteria, and the authorities do not accept that a nanny, housekeeper, chauffeur or non medical carer meets that standard. New applications for non EU domestic staff are almost always refused. Two narrow exceptions exist. The first is the executive relocation route. The second is the hiring of a non EU national already living in Switzerland whose existing permit allows household employment, which covers spouses of Swiss and EU nationals, recognised refugees, students within their permitted hours and certain B permit holders not tied to one employer. The relocation exception is the one worth understanding in detail, because it is the only route a career in private service can actually open. It applies where a family moving to Switzerland brings a long serving household employee with them. The worker must show at least two years of prior employment with that family abroad, supported by documentary evidence: employment contracts, payslips, payroll or tax records. A Swiss compliant contract covering duties, salary, hours, insurance and accommodation, drawn in line with the relevant Normalarbeitsvertrag, must accompany the file. Approval is discretionary and cantonal, and processing runs from several weeks to a few months. If granted, the permit is usually an employer specific L, renewable, with a B permit possible for longer assignments. The employer obligations that follow are those of a small business. A written contract is mandatory, the NAV minimum salary cannot be waived, and board and lodging for live in staff may be credited only at the legally fixed value. Cantons typically expect from 40 to 43 hours a week, clear off duty time, at least one full day off weekly and proper overtime compensation, with a private, habitable room provided free of charge. Registration and contributions are required for AHV, IV and EO, for unemployment insurance, for accident insurance including non occupational cover above eight hours a week, and for the second pillar where income reaches the threshold. Withholding tax is calculated and paid monthly for foreign workers without a C permit. Routing the employment through a family office simplifies payroll and changes nothing at all for immigration: the authorities assess the real duties, not the job title on the contract.
articles.why: For a candidate outside the EU, the Swiss door opens mainly on service already given and properly recorded. Keeping contracts, payslips, references and dates of employment in order is not paperwork, it is the permit application.

articles.title: One operator now runs three of the terminals at Van Nuys, and the ground crew meeting the family answers to a single name
articles.body:
On 15 September, Signature Aviation announced the acquisition of Castle and Cooke Aviation Services at Van Nuys Airport. The purchase takes Signature from two fixed base operators on the field to three, and the former Castle and Cooke terminal has been redesignated VNY North within the Signature network. The company said the deal expands its Southern California presence, increases capacity and improves access for customers travelling through the Los Angeles region. Tony Lefebvre, Signature's chief executive, described Van Nuys as one of the most important business aviation markets in the world.

That description is not marketing. Van Nuys is among the busiest business aviation airports anywhere and the principal private gateway into Los Angeles, which is why a change of ownership on that particular field carries weight well beyond one terminal. The transaction also sits inside a broader pattern: capital is flowing into aviation infrastructure rather than only into aircraft, on the view that airport adjacent assets are long duration investments tied to the health of the sector as a whole. The effects pull in two directions. Less competition on a field can put upward pressure on pricing, while added hangar capacity at secondary airports acts as a relief valve.

For anyone arranging a principal's movements, the practical consequences arrive faster than the strategic ones. Charter operators, brokers and flight departments build preferences around specific providers on the basis of service levels, ramp access, fuel programmes and hangar availability. When ownership changes, those variables change with it, and airport preference follows. The terminal a family has used for a decade may now sit under a different network, with different handling standards, different scheduling and a different name on the arrivals card.
articles.why: A change of terminal ownership decides who meets the car at the gate, which hangar the aircraft sleeps in and how quickly the family clears the ramp. Anyone building an itinerary into Los Angeles should know whose name is now on the building.

articles.title: Art Basel returns to the Grand Palais with 211 galleries and a new director, and the invitation only preview falls on 20 October
articles.body:
Art Basel has published the exhibitor list for its fifth Paris edition, which runs at the Grand Palais from 23 to 25 October. The fair brings together 211 exhibitors from 41 countries and territories across its three sectors, Galeries, Emergence and Premise, with nearly 30 galleries taking part in Paris for the first time. More than 60 of the exhibitors operate spaces in France, a proportion that explains much of the fair's character, and the list otherwise spans Europe, the Americas, Asia, Africa and the Middle East, including houses from Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Turkey, Lebanon, Indonesia, South Africa, Nigeria, Cote d'Ivoire and Tunisia.

The calendar around the fair matters as much as the fair itself. Preview days fall on 21 and 22 October, with a public vernissage on 22 October. Avant Premiere, the invitation only preview reserved for galleries and their principal clients, returns for a second year on 20 October. Oh La La, the fair's signature rehang, in which a guest collaborator from outside the art world reorganises the booths, takes place on 23 and 24 October. A record 12 joint booth presentations appear in the main sector this year, and the Public Program returns in partnership with Parisian institutions, with Miu Miu as its official partner.

This is the first edition under Karim Crippa, who succeeded the fair's inaugural director. It opens against a recovering domestic market. According to the Art Basel and UBS Global Art Market Report 2026, sales in France reached USD 4.5 billion in 2025, a rise of 9 per cent year on year after two years of contraction and a return above 2019 levels. France now accounts for 8 per cent of the global art market, ranking fourth worldwide and first within the European Union, where it represents more than half the market by value.
articles.why: Paris fair week is one of the fixed points of the autumn diary, and the dates are not interchangeable. Knowing that 20 October is the invitation only day, and 22 October the public one, is the difference between a principal arriving with access and arriving with a crowd.

briefs.b: CAE's workforce forecast projects a need for 102,000 new business aviation professionals globally by 2034, of whom 69,000 are maintenance technicians. The figure was cited this week alongside a Fortune Business Insights projection that the global charter market will approach USD 48.2 billion by 2034. Maintenance capacity, not fleet size, is increasingly the constraint on availability.

For 2026 the Internal Revenue Service sets the household employee threshold at USD 3,000 in cash wages. Cross it and every dollar paid to that employee for the year becomes social security and Medicare wages, at a combined 15.3 per cent, up to a social security wage base of USD 184,500. Separately, paying USD 1,000 or more in any calendar quarter triggers federal unemployment tax.

Sotheby's has opened its Important Watches sale in Geneva for 8 November, with viewing from 5 to 7 November at the Mandarin Oriental on Quai Turrettini. The house is still accepting consignments, so no lots or estimates are published yet. The sale follows record results in May and sits at the head of the Geneva November week.

lead.title: Greece will charge non EU buyers five times the transfer tax from January, and the bill on an Athens purchase rises by 96,000 euros overnight
lead.standfirst: The Prime Minister announced the increase at the Thessaloniki International Fair this month, and every investor on the country's residence programme is by definition inside its scope.
lead.body:
Speaking at the 90th Thessaloniki International Fair earlier this month, Kyriakos Mitsotakis told his audience that alongside the incentives in his housing package there would also be a disincentive. Greece will raise its property transfer tax from 3 per cent to 15 per cent for buyers from third countries outside the European Union, with effect from 1 January 2027. Interest from buyers in countries such as China, Turkey and Israel, he said, may to a degree be welcome, but it has made it much harder for Greeks in several areas to acquire homes of their own.

The arithmetic is unambiguous. Under the current regime the transfer tax stands at 3 per cent, an effective 3.09 per cent once the municipal surcharge is added, charged on whichever is higher of the agreed price or the property's state assessed objective value, and paid by the buyer before the notarial deed is signed. An 800,000 euro purchase in Athens or Thessaloniki, the minimum in the residence programme's high demand zone, currently carries roughly 24,000 euros of transfer tax. From 2027 that bill reaches 120,000 euros. A 400,000 euro acquisition elsewhere in Greece rises from 12,000 to 60,000 euros, and a 250,000 euro conversion or restoration project from 7,500 to 37,500 euros. The measure sits inside a package worth 2.2 billion euros that also carries a 2 billion euro subsidised mortgage programme, phased cuts to electricity costs and the abolition of the ENFIA annual property tax in small settlements.

A second deadline compounds the first. Greece's suspension of 24 per cent VAT on new build purchases, which has channelled foreign buyers towards the transfer tax instead, is currently due to lapse at the end of 2026 unless it is extended again. Until the implementing bill is published, several questions stay open: whether third country nationals who already hold Greek residence permits fall within scope, how purchases made through Greek or EU companies are treated, and whether transactions already under way receive transitional protection.

The measure is not uncontested. Alexander Risvas of the Athens firm Risvas & Associates argues that foreign investment should not become the convenient explanation for a structural housing problem, pointing to IMF findings that roughly 35 per cent of Greece's housing stock is not used as a primary residence and to Greek housing investment running at about 60 per cent of the EU average. He notes that apartment prices rose 8.1 per cent in 2025 and a further 5.7 per cent year on year in the first quarter of 2026, per Bank of Greece figures, yet Eurostat data show Greek housing costs moving from 8 per cent below the EU average in 2010 to approximately 29 per cent below it in 2024. A regime under which two buyers pay 3 per cent and 15 per cent on the same property, on the same date, on the basis of citizenship alone raises questions of equal treatment under Article 4(5) of the Greek Constitution, and Strasbourg case law holds that differences in treatment based exclusively on nationality require very weighty reasons.

The timing is political. Mitsotakis's speech was his last address to the fair before national elections due in spring 2027, and the 15 per cent rate would take effect shortly before Greeks go to the polls. For households already holding or contemplating a Greek property, the practical horizon is now measured in weeks rather than years.
lead.why: Where a family buys decides where its staff will be posted, and a tax cliff dated 1 January concentrates a great many decisions into one autumn. Whoever runs the houses should expect a property to be opened, surveyed, staffed or closed on a legislative calendar rather than a seasonal one.

articles.title: New York pays household staff weekly, by law, and the paperwork behind that rule now carries its own penalties
articles.body:
New York treats a private house as a workplace and its domestic staff as W-2 employees, with protections set out in the Domestic Workers' Bill of Rights at Labor Law section 161-A. For 2026 the minimum wage stands at USD 17.00 an hour in New York City, Long Island and Westchester County, and USD 16.00 across the rest of the state, the last of the scheduled increases before rates are tied to regional inflation from 2027.

Overtime is where the state parts company with federal law. Federal rules exempt live-in domestic workers from overtime altogether. New York does not: a live-out employee is paid time and a half beyond 40 hours in a week, a live-in employee beyond 44, and any work performed on the agreed day of rest is paid at the same premium. The household owes one period of 24 consecutive hours of rest each week. On a 24 hour shift, common for a live-in nanny or an overnight carer, only 13 hours need be paid, but that concession holds only where the employee receives 8 hours of sleep with at least 5 of them uninterrupted and 3 hours of meal breaks. Where sleep is broken or the breaks are not given, the full 24 hours are payable.

The pay rhythm is fixed. Under Labor Law section 191(1)(a), domestic workers count as manual workers and must be paid weekly, with wages due within seven calendar days of the end of the week in which they were earned. Section 195(3) requires an itemised pay stub with each payment, showing period dates, gross wages, total hours with overtime separated, both rates, every deduction, net pay and the employer's details, and the records are kept for six years. The 2025 amendment to section 191 gave the rule teeth: a first violation is capped at 100 per cent of the lost interest on delayed wages, while subsequent violations carry liquidated damages equal to 100 per cent of the wages owed, with a six year limitation period. Failure to issue the LS-54 wage notice at hire, or whenever pay changes, can cost up to USD 50 a working day, capped at USD 5,000 per employee, plus costs.

Insurance sits outside payroll and is frequently the gap. Workers' compensation is required for any live-in employee whatever the hours, and for anyone working 40 hours or more a week. Disability benefits and Paid Family Leave cover is required at 20 hours a week and 30 days in a year, and for that test the state counts all the time the employer requires the worker's presence, including sleeping, eating and on-call hours at the residence. Two days away with a member of staff required on site therefore counts as 48 hours. Operating without required workers' compensation cover can trigger fines of USD 2,000 for every ten days of non compliance, and deducting the premium from an employee's wages is a misdemeanour under section 31. For 2026 the Paid Family Leave premium runs at 0.432 per cent of gross wages, capped at USD 411.91 a year, against a maximum benefit of USD 1,228.53 a week for up to twelve weeks.

One requirement is new this year. From tax year 2026, employers must report qualified overtime compensation separately on Form W-2, in Box 12 under code TT, transitional relief having applied for 2025. It follows the federal deduction introduced by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, under which an employee may deduct the premium half of qualifying overtime from taxable income, up to USD 12,500 for a single filer and USD 25,000 jointly, phasing out above USD 150,000 of modified adjusted gross income, for tax years 2025 to 2028. The figure only reaches the employee's return if the hours were recorded correctly in the house.
articles.why: Every one of these numbers begins as a line on a rota or a time sheet kept by whoever runs the household. A house manager who can produce a current wage notice, a weekly itemised stub and a clean record of hours is the reason the principal is not exposed.

articles.title: China has written down its power to stop its own citizens leaving, and the principal may only discover the ban at the airport
articles.body:
China's new exit and entry regulation came into force on Monday, widening the grounds on which Chinese citizens can be barred from leaving. Premier Li Qiang signed Order No. 841 on 22 July, and its nineteen articles now govern everything from overseas safety warnings to the conduct of emigration intermediaries.

Article 4 sets out three circumstances in which authorities may stop a citizen at the border. Anyone who has served administrative detention for fraudulently obtaining travel documents, or for illegally crossing a border, faces a ban of six months to three years once the penalty ends. Criminal activity abroad judged to damage national security or interests carries the same range, the clock starting on return to China. A third ground concerns breaches of export control or technology transfer rules that may endanger industrial or technological security, decided by the commerce authorities, and for this category the text sets no time limit at all. Authorities must notify the individual in writing of the facts, reasons and legal basis, but Article 6 permits silence where notice might affect national security or a criminal investigation, which is precisely the ground the new rules expand. Citizens have no way to check whether a ban applies to them. Most would learn of one only at the border. Foreign nationals, for their part, face entry bans of one to five years for supplying false information in a visa or entry application.

Enforcement was rising well before the regulation was signed. Data shared with the BBC by the rights group Safeguard Defenders show mentions of exit bans in China's supreme court database rising from 89 in 2016 to 188,760 in 2025. Over roughly the same period the share of civil verdicts dealing with exit bans grew more than thirtyfold, from about 0.23 per cent to 7.3 per cent. In March, the co-founders of the artificial intelligence company Manus were barred from leaving while regulators reviewed a USD 2 billion acquisition of their firm.

The relevance to the private world is one of scale. Chinese nationals held 10,593 initial investor permits under the Greek residence programme as of February 2026, 48.1 per cent of the total and more than three times the Turkish share. At the last detailed count in Portugal, in 2023, Chinese investors had received 44 per cent of all residence permits issued since that programme opened in 2012. In the United States, freedom of information data published in January show mainland Chinese investors filing roughly half of all EB-5 petitions since the 2022 reform. David Lesperance, who advises ultra high net worth families on tax and citizenship planning, reports clients choosing to leave, as he puts it, before the knock on the door, on the reasoning that in China the tax authorities do not send letters.

The operational consequences are concrete and unglamorous. An individual under an undisclosed ban may be unable to attend a biometrics appointment, complete a purchase in person, or satisfy a physical presence requirement, and neither he nor his advisers will necessarily know until he reaches the border. On the China side, domestic emigration agencies must register with immigration authorities by mid December, and overseas firms may no longer sell exit and entry services directly inside the country.
articles.why: An itinerary is not secure because a passport is valid. Anyone building a family's travel should hold a second plan for the leg that depends on one person clearing an exit control, and should know which appointments genuinely require that person to be present.

articles.title: Christie's marks forty years in Asia with a Basquiat skull and the first Kusama pumpkin offered since her death
articles.body: Christie's holds its 20th and 21st century marquee auctions in Hong Kong on 29 and 30 September, at the firm's Asia Pacific headquarters on the sixth floor of The Henderson in Central. The sales form part of a year long programme marking forty years of the house operating in Asia, and the works are on public view from 22 to 29 September. The evening sale on 29 September is led by Jean-Michel Basquiat's Ancient Scientist of 1984, a large mixed media composition in acrylic, oilstick and Xerox paper collage on canvas carrying the artist's most enduring motif, a human skull. The estimate runs from HK$56 million to HK$76 million, or USD 7.1 million to USD 9.7 million. Beside it stands Yayoi Kusama's A-Pumpkin (YHP) of 2011, estimated at HK$48 million to HK$68 million, USD 6.1 million to USD 8.7 million. Kusama died in August at the age of 97, and the large canvas, a yellow pumpkin in black polka dots set against a prismatic Infinity Net ground, is among the first significant examples to reach the rostrum since. Asian modernism is represented by Zao Wou-Ki's Voie lactée, 09.11.56, from the Chinese French painter's Oracle Bone period, estimated at HK$45 million to HK$75 million. Chu Teh-Chun's Automne of 1985 makes its auction debut at HK$25 million to HK$35 million, a large diptych and the only snow scene in the artist's Snow Landscape series rendered in an autumn palette. Liu Ye's Blue Sea of 1998, among his largest naval paintings, is estimated at HK$16 million to HK$26 million. The Western material is led by Paul Cezanne's L'Assiette bleue at HK$25 million to HK$35 million, Gerhard Richter's Abstraktes Bild of 1991, one of only 27 red dominant abstractions he made that year, at HK$38 million to HK$55 million, and Henri Matisse's Jeune femme au canape of 1944 at HK$20 million to HK$30 million. The day sales on 30 September widen the field. The 21st century session is headed by Yoshitomo Nara's Q&A of 1995, estimated at HK$12 million to HK$18 million, with a smaller Kusama pumpkin of 2003 at HK$9 million to HK$12 million, alongside works by Christine Ay Tjoe, Jonas Wood and Andy Warhol. A single owner grouping, Between Worlds, runs across both the evening and day auctions. What the calendar records is the steady consolidation of Hong Kong as the autumn fixture in the collecting year, and the widening of what an Asian sale means: a Basquiat and a Cezanne offered in the same room as Chu Teh-Chun and Wu Guanzhong, priced for the same audience.
articles.why: A principal bidding in Hong Kong sets off a chain that runs through the household: shipping and customs, condition reports on arrival, a wall or a store found, and the schedule on the insurance policy amended before the work is hung.

articles.title: The Monaco show opens on Wednesday with a third of its fleet shown by brokers rather than builders
articles.body:
The 35th Monaco Yacht Show runs in Port Hercule from Wednesday 23 to Saturday 26 September. The organisers expect around 120 superyachts, of which 43 were delivered during 2026, and more than 30,000 visitors across the four days.

The composition of the fleet has shifted in a way worth noting. As of publication of the official lists, 38 of the confirmed yachts are presented not by the yards that built them but by brokerage and charter firms, an in service fleet rather than a new build showcase. The 2026 programme has been expanded to admit brokerage and yacht management companies as exhibitors in their own right, which formalises something the quayside had already become: the week in which next season's charter availability, and its pricing, is effectively settled.

Tenders have been given unusual prominence this year, with more than 60 on display. The category has moved a long way from a functional craft slung on a davit. Owners and charter guests now judge a tender on range, comfort, design and capability, and it is increasingly specified as an extension of life on board rather than a means of reaching the shore. For anyone arranging days out from a yacht, the tender is the piece of equipment that determines what is actually possible from an anchorage.

The exhibitor material also points to where the technical conversation has gone: propulsion, energy management, emissions reduction, water treatment and digital systems, with sustainability now sitting inside the commercial discussion rather than beside it. The show has run an environmental programme since 2005, but the subject has moved from the seminar rooms onto the specification sheets.

For the private household, the show is less a spectacle than a marketplace of people. Brokers, managers, captains and crew agencies are all in the same three hundred metres of quay for four days, which is why placements, charters and refit decisions cluster around this week in the calendar.
articles.why: A concierge booking next summer is choosing from the fleet lying alongside this week, and from the brokers standing in front of it. Knowing which boats are in service, who manages them and what tender each carries is the difference between an itinerary that works and one that is merely booked.

briefs.b: Rolex will offer four one of a kind Cosmograph Daytonas at Phillips in London on 28 September, each corresponding to a season. The cases are 18ct yellow, Everose or white gold, or platinum, with dials cut from natural stone, gem set bezels and diamond set lugs and crown guards. Proceeds are split between the Federer Foundation and Re:wild, and no estimates had been published when the sale was announced.

The Netherlands has abandoned its plan for a 36 per cent tax on unrealised gains and will instead propose a model charged only at the point of sale. Dutch investors keep the existing notional return system until at least 2029 while the replacement is drafted. It is the second European government this month to revise how it taxes internationally mobile capital.

Business jet deliveries reached 383 aircraft in the first half of 2026, up 8.2 per cent on the same period last year. Total general and business aviation billings rose 15.5 per cent to USD 14.3 billion on 1,458 aircraft shipped, a rise of 1.7 per cent by volume. The gap between the two figures is the market moving towards larger and more expensive aeroplanes.

lead.title: A single wildfire score now decides whether the mountain house can be insured at all, and the people who run it sit inside the file
lead.standfirst: Colorado's disclosure law took effect this summer as carriers retreated from the resort valleys, and documented mitigation has become the difference between a policy and a refusal.
lead.body:
Since 1 July 2026, under Colorado's House Bill 25-1182, every insurer writing a home in the state must disclose the wildfire risk score it used to rate that property, give the owner a route to contest it, and credit documented mitigation against it. The score itself is produced by one of a small number of models, Verisk FireLine, CoreLogic or ZestyAI Z-FIRE depending on the carrier, and in the Roaring Fork Valley it has become the single number that determines whether a house is placed with an admitted insurer, moved to the surplus lines market at a multiple of the price, or declined outright. Pitkin County adopted the state aligned wildfire hazard map in 2025 alongside the Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code, and parcels the county had long classified as low hazard were reclassified upwards without anything on the ground changing.

The retreat of the carriers is not theoretical. Insurers are non renewing or declining new business across Aspen, Vail, Telluride and Steamboat Springs over concentrated wildfire exposure. United Policyholders documented one Colorado case in which a client's USD 20 million of buildings cover, previously written on a single policy at USD 60,000 a year, was non renewed and had to be rebuilt across four separate policies totalling USD 600,000 in combined premium. The state backstop offers no shelter at this level: the Colorado FAIR Plan caps residential cover at USD 750,000, paid at actual cash value, and only for fire, lightning and smoke.

Underneath the placement sits a second problem, which is that the sum insured on most of these houses is wrong. Custom construction in the Roaring Fork Valley runs from USD 800 to USD 1,500 per square foot, so a house of 6,000 square feet costs from USD 4.8 million to USD 9 million to rebuild. Sale prices move on entirely different logic: Aspen's median single family sale price reached USD 17.5 million in 2025, up 31 per cent in a year, and Snowmass Village's reached USD 8.25 million, up 11 per cent. A dwelling limit copied from a purchase price or a stale appraisal is the most common and most expensive error on these files.

Occupancy is underwritten as heavily as fire. A large share of Aspen and Snowmass houses stand empty for months, which means an undiscovered frozen pipe or an evacuation with nobody on site. Most private client carriers now require a central water shutoff with low temperature monitoring bound as a policy condition, prefer to write the primary residence and the mountain house together, and price the vacancy months upward where there is no one in residence. Pitkin County runs a free professional wildfire risk assessment, roughly two hours on site with a written mitigation report delivered within fifteen days, and that report is precisely the documentation the new law obliges insurers to credit.

The practical consequence is that the house's insurability is now assembled from evidence that only the household can produce: defensible space maintained to code, a Class A roof and ember resistant vents recorded, the water shutoff tested, the assessment report filed, the contents schedule current, and somebody who can be at the property within the hour.
lead.why: Defensible space, a monitored water shutoff, a current inventory and a caretaker on site are underwriting facts now, not housekeeping. Whoever keeps that record is the reason a policy is offered, priced or withdrawn.

articles.title: The four hundred wealthiest Americans are now worth USD 8 trillion, and the price of admission has never been higher
articles.body:
Forbes published the 45th edition of its Forbes 400 on 15 September. The four hundred richest people in the United States are collectively worth a record USD 8 trillion, up USD 1.4 trillion on last year's list. The threshold to appear at all is USD 4.4 billion, a record in its own right and USD 600 million higher than the cut off twelve months ago.

At the top the concentration is extreme. Elon Musk holds first place for the fifth consecutive year at USD 908 billion, having more than doubled his fortune over the year. Jeff Bezos is second at USD 378 billion and Larry Page of Alphabet third at USD 278 billion. Between them, the three account for roughly a fifth of the entire list.

The more revealing figure sits below the line. A record 590 American billionaires were not wealthy enough to qualify, among them names as publicly conspicuous as Oprah Winfrey and Taylor Swift. Ten figure fortunes have become numerous enough that they no longer distinguish anyone, which is a reasonable description of the American employer market as it now stands.

For the private household, the shape of the list matters more than its arithmetic. A deepening tier of billionaires who fall outside the first four hundred is the tier that buys second and third residences, establishes single family offices, and staffs them. That is the population from which most private service appointments in the United States are made, and it grew again this year.
articles.why: The American market sets the ceiling for private service pay in most roles. A wider band of billionaire households below the very top is where the volume of estate, chef and chief of staff appointments actually comes from.

articles.title: A charter broker has paused every flight for thirty days, and roughly USD 150 million of prepaid client money is exposed
articles.body:
OneFlight International, the charter broker behind the BAJit jet card, halted all flight activity on 15 September, telling customers the pause would run for the next thirty days or until further notice while it evaluates its operations. Private Jet Card Comparisons, which first reported the halt, estimates that around USD 150 million in prepaid card balances and booked flight value is now exposed. OneFlight sells cards with deposits starting at USD 100,000 and owns no aircraft, arranging every flight through third party operators.

The strain was visible before the pause. In August the company told card holders they faced a 35 per cent economic surcharge, citing extraordinary economic pressures in private aviation, then withdrew it after customer objection. On 9 September a company vice president wrote that the chief executive was actively addressing financial and operational issues that had developed under the previous finance director. Several charter operators say they are owed money, one reporting USD 250,000 outstanding on a recent flight, while others report being paid as recently as August. OneFlight recorded USD 232 million of revenue in 2025, up 90 per cent year on year.

The structural point is the one worth carrying forward. A prepaid jet card deposit held by a broker is very rarely kept in escrow, separate from the company's operating cash. It functions as an unsecured loan to that company, and in an insolvency the card holder queues behind secured lenders and administrative costs. The precedent is documented: when JetSuite grounded its fleet in 2020, SuiteKey card holders were told to expect between 2.3 per cent and 15 per cent of their claims, and the payments that eventually arrived came closer to half a cent on the dollar.

Competitors have moved within days. FlyUSA launched a USD 100 million recovery programme for stranded customers, offering a complimentary membership with no new deposit and 20 per cent of qualifying flight spend returned as credit up to the value of a verified stranded balance. Amalfi Jets has waived its usual USD 100,000 deposit for current and former OneFlight members until 15 October.
articles.why: Whoever books the family's flights is choosing a counterparty, not just a price. Two questions belong on the file before any deposit is wired: will it be held in escrow, and does the company own the aircraft it puts you on.

articles.title: The largest single offering of Willett ever brought to auction closes today, inside Sotheby's first wine and spirits festival
articles.body:
Sotheby's is staging its inaugural Nightcap Wine and Spirits Festival at the Breuer building in New York from 16 to 19 September. The whisky centrepiece is the Whisky and Whiskey sale, which has run since 3 September and closes today, and which is led by The Wax Top Collection: 328 bottles, the single largest offering of Willett Family Estate ever brought to auction at one time.

Willett is the label that turned American whiskey into a collecting category rather than a drinking one, and the wax sealed bottlings that give the collection its name are the most closely tracked expressions in that market. Around them the sale offers more than 250 further lots spanning pre Prohibition and Prohibition era American whiskey, rare Scotch and Japanese single malts, which is a fair map of where spirits collecting has moved over the past decade.

One lot sits slightly apart. A Bowmore ARC-54, a 54 year old Islay malt distilled in 1968 and bottled at 44.3 per cent, carries an estimate from USD 40,000 to USD 60,000, with proceeds benefiting The Foundation of Hope.

The practical relevance is that spirits are now handled with the documentary rigour long applied to wine and pictures. Bottles at these levels are scheduled on an insurance policy, and their value depends on fill level, label condition, storage temperature and an unbroken record of custody. A house with a serious spirits room is holding a catalogued asset, and the person who signs for deliveries is the first link in its provenance.
articles.why: Cellars and spirits rooms are inventoried assets. Condition, storage and chain of custody are recorded by whoever runs the residence, and they determine what a bottle is worth when it is next valued or sold.

articles.title: The Standard's old address on Sunset returns this month as a 137 room house, behind USD 116.5 million of fresh debt
articles.body:
Ian Schrager and Ed Scheetz have secured USD 116.5 million of bridge financing for Public Hotel West Hollywood, the 137 key property at 8300 Sunset Boulevard that is due to open this month on the site of the former Standard. Driftwood Capital and Benefit Street Partners provided the loan, negotiated by Cushman and Wakefield, and it was reported on 8 September.

The pair bought the site for USD 112.5 million in early 2023, two years after the Standard closed, and have run a ground up renovation since. Guest rooms and suites have been redesigned and the amenity programme now includes a new rooftop deck and a nightclub, in a building Schrager developed with the British architect John Pawson.

The reopening matters chiefly as a signal about the Sunset Strip, which spent several years without an anchor address after the Standard went dark. Schrager's stated position on the Public brand is accessible pricing attached to design, service and social space, which puts the house in a different register from the private club model that has dominated recent Los Angeles openings.

For a household with a Los Angeles diary, the Strip returning to use changes the geography of an evening. It is one address, in a city where the map of where people actually go is rewritten every couple of seasons.
articles.why: Knowing which houses are opening, and where they sit on the map a principal actually uses, is part of the standing brief. It is the difference between booking a table and choosing one.

briefs.t: Heavy jets pull away from the rest
briefs.b: Global Jet Capital's forecast to 2030 has pre owned heavy jet transactions growing 4.9 per cent a year while light and medium volumes barely move. Large cabin aircraft currently sell in a median of 78 days against 134 for mid size, available inventory sits at 6.6 per cent of the active fleet against a historical average near 10 per cent, and manufacturer backlog has risen 12.8 per cent in six months to USD 66.8 billion.

The London Design Festival runs from 12 to 20 September across eleven districts, with Soho taking part for the first time and Shoreditch Design Week the largest district on the schedule. The Design Museum's programme includes the first retrospective devoted to NIGO, artistic director of KENZO.

briefs.t: Ski homes up 23 per cent in five years
briefs.b: Knight Frank's Alpine Property Report records prime ski homes rising 23 per cent on average over the past five years, a period in which several major prime markets slowed. Courchevel 1850 remains the French benchmark, while Verbier has effectively plateaued after several strong years.
