lead.title: Dubai is taking Britain's estate managers, head chefs and senior nannies, and the offer it makes is not simply a bigger number
lead.standfirst: A London agency with nearly thirty years of placements has set out, role by role, how Gulf households are recruiting the most experienced British private staff, and what the arithmetic actually looks like on both sides.
lead.body:
Eden Private Staff published a long note on 1 September describing what it calls the Dubai effect, the growing ability of Dubai and the wider Gulf to recruit experienced, English speaking household professionals directly from London, the Home Counties, British country estates and internationally mobile European households. The agency is careful about the shape of it. This is not a general movement of every domestic employee. It is targeted competition for proven senior people who can enter a complex household and perform with limited supervision, and it falls on three roles above all: estate managers and estate directors, head chefs and senior private chefs, and senior nannies, including Norland trained, multilingual and travelling professionals.

The numbers explain the pull, though not in the way a principal might expect. Indicative British salaries for an estate manager or estate director now run from about GBP 110,000 to GBP 220,000 and beyond, depending on the number of properties, staff headcount, capital projects, budget authority, security and travel. In Monaco and the South of France, significant appointments may be quoted at about EUR 8,500 to EUR 16,000 net per month, frequently with accommodation and bonus. Dubai packages are quoted differently again, as tax free cash with housing, healthcare, visa, annual flights and relocation sitting outside the stated figure, which makes a direct comparison with a British gross salary almost meaningless unless all three are rebuilt on the same basis.

The agency works one example through. A senior nanny on GBP 140,000 gross in England or Wales takes home roughly GBP 86,000 on 2026/27 income tax and National Insurance rates, excluding pension and student loan; employer National Insurance alone can lift the household's cash cost to about GBP 160,250 before pension and benefits. At a late August rate of about AED 5 to the pound, a Dubai salary of AED 430,000 is also worth about GBP 86,000, except that the UAE levies no personal income tax on individuals and the housing, health insurance and flights may be supplied in addition. The point is not that every Gulf offer is better. It is that a principal can no longer defend a position by naming the gross figure.

Chefs are the most transferable of the three. British guidance places private chefs broadly between GBP 65,000 and GBP 125,000, with head chefs in demanding principal households reaching about GBP 110,000 to GBP 190,000 and above, while Eden's own directional figures put executive estate chefs at GBP 120,000 to GBP 200,000 and above. Dubai equivalents run from about AED 240,000 to AED 360,000 for a family private chef, AED 360,000 to AED 600,000 and above for a Michelin trained chef, and AED 480,000 to AED 720,000 and above for an executive estate chef. Even so, the agency's argument is that where a British role demands permanent flexibility and provides no rota, no second chef and no structured time away, Dubai does not need to offer dramatically more money. It only needs to offer a more sustainable life.

What leaves with the person is the real exposure. A long serving estate manager holds years of knowledge about properties, budgets, contractors, security arrangements and family preferences. A head chef understands every dietary requirement, medical consideration and entertaining standard. A senior nanny holds continuity across schools, residences, travel and the stages of a childhood. The recommended answer is unglamorous and mostly administrative: benchmark total reward rather than base salary, review compensation on a timetable rather than after a resignation, write a five year plan for each critical seat, align authority with accountability, and conduct stay interviews with the people a household cannot afford to lose.
lead.why: A package is now read as a whole, not as a headline salary. Anyone entering private service should learn to price accommodation, healthcare, flights, rota and relief alongside the figure on the contract, and to describe the scope of a role rather than its title.

articles.title: Twenty nine fortunes now hold more than a quarter of all billionaire wealth, and one in five of the people behind them lives in a country they were not born in
articles.body:
Altrata published the thirteenth edition of its Billionaire Census on 27 August. The global billionaire population grew 8.2 per cent year on year to 3,795 individuals, the strongest annual expansion in five years, capping a decade in which the class has grown by almost 60 per cent. Total billionaire wealth rose 12.8 per cent to a record USD 15.1 trillion, equal to nearly a quarter of the total market capitalisation of the S&P 500 in 2025.

The concentration inside that figure is the more striking finding. Twenty nine superbillionaires, each with a fortune above USD 50 billion, now account for 27.2 per cent of all billionaire wealth, close to four times their 7.2 per cent share in 2017, when only ten people held fortunes of that size. Altrata attributes much of the acceleration to artificial intelligence: among the 150 listed companies contributing most to billionaire wealth, those making meaningful AI investments saw valuations climb 23 per cent faster than those that did not across 2024 and 2025.

For a household, the useful numbers are the ones about people rather than markets. One in five billionaires was born outside the country in which they now live, and the variation by city is wide: about 60 per cent of billionaires in London are foreign born, one of the highest shares of any major global city, against 19 per cent in New York and 41 per cent in San Francisco. Singapore and Hong Kong also stand out, while China, Germany and India show far lower shares, reflecting domestic and family owned business roots.

Two further findings bear directly on private service. Over the next decade some USD 6.6 trillion of billionaire wealth will pass on, with almost 5,000 direct heirs, spouses and adult children, expected to receive a sizeable share; women will account for a significant proportion of those beneficiaries, including 90 per cent of spouses. And the value of billionaire holdings in fine art, sports teams, luxury cars, yachts, private jets, watches and jewellery has grown by an average of 13.3 per cent a year per billionaire over the past decade. Sport is the single most popular interest among billionaires, with more than 200 of them, just over 5 per cent, now holding a direct stake in a team or franchise.
articles.why: The objects a household stores, insures, moves and prepares are appreciating faster than most portfolios, and the person who will give instructions about them in ten years is frequently not the person giving them today.

articles.title: There will be 1,747 branded residences by 2032, and each one sells a version of the service a private household has always employed people to provide
articles.body:
Savills has published its annual branded residences report for 2025 and 2026. The global total of completed schemes is expected to reach about 910 by the end of 2025, up from 764 in December 2024, a rise of 19 per cent in a single year. Measured from 323 schemes in 2015, the sector has almost tripled in a decade, a compound annual growth rate of 10.9 per cent that exceeds growth in both the global hospitality and real estate sectors over the same period.

The pipeline is not a forecast but a contracted figure. A further 837 projects are already signed and scheduled for delivery by 2032, which would bring the world total to 1,747. During 2025 alone, 25 countries saw their first branded residential scheme, and 39 new hotel brands and 19 new non hotel brands entered the sector. Growth over the past five years has been strongest in Asia Pacific, at 55 per cent, supported by pipelines in Vietnam, Thailand and India, and in the Middle East and North Africa, at 187 per cent, led by Dubai and the wider Gulf.

What the buyer is paying for is service made permanent and built into the freehold: concierge, housekeeping, security, maintenance and food and beverage supplied by an operator rather than assembled by the owner. Analysis of the sector puts the global price premium at roughly a third over comparable unbranded stock, justified by amenities, scarcity and the resale confidence a brand is thought to confer. Standalone schemes with no attached hotel have risen from about 15 per cent of new announcements in 2018 to more than 40 per cent, which means the operator increasingly arrives without a hotel behind it.

None of this removes private staff from the picture; it changes what they do. In a branded apartment, a house manager spends less time recruiting and supervising a full household team and more time managing an operator's service level agreement, negotiating access, protecting privacy inside a building that keeps records, and covering the gap between a standardised offer and a family's actual habits. The families most likely to hold such a residence are also the ones most likely to hold three or four other addresses where service is still assembled the old way.
articles.why: A growing share of the addresses a principal owns will come with service attached. Knowing how to hold an operator to a written standard, and where that standard stops, is becoming part of the house manager's brief.

articles.title: The largest private aviation company has stopped selling the product most families start with, and the entry point to flying private has narrowed
articles.body:
NetJets has paused all new sales of its 25 hour jet cards and its 25 hour per year leases, citing record high retention rates and demand for its fractional shares. Existing card holders may buy a renewal card, and existing 25 hour lease holders may either start another lease or purchase a card, but the products are closed to newcomers. The company said its aim was to focus on its core business of shared ownership and to avoid compromising service delivery to existing card, lease and share owners.

The decision follows six years of heavy expansion. NetJets has added more than 350 net new aircraft to its fractional fleet over that period and expects to take 80 more jets in 2026, with recent additions including the Praetor 500, the Citation Ascend and the Bombardier Global 8000. In the first six months of 2026 its flight numbers grew 11.8 per cent on the same period a year earlier.

The wider data explains why the card was the product to sacrifice. WINGX figures compiled by SherpaReport show fractional departures up 11.5 per cent in the first half of 2026, at 396,600 flights, or 20.3 per cent of all business jet departures worldwide. Flexjet grew 11.0 per cent. Over the same period branded charter, the segment that includes jet card programmes, fell 3.1 per cent, corporate flight departments contracted 8.9 per cent, and private flight departments operating aircraft for a single owner grew 12.4 per cent. Demand is moving towards committed, contracted access and away from pay as you go.

This is not the first pause. NetJets suspended card sales in 2021 during the pandemic surge, introduced a 25 hour three year lease in mid 2022 and restarted card sales late that year with tighter peak day rules. The immediate consequence for anyone arranging travel is narrower choice at the entry level and a stronger case for comparing the remaining card providers early, rather than at the point a family needs a seat.
articles.why: The person who books the aircraft is usually the person who discovers, at short notice, that a programme has closed. Knowing which access model a household actually holds, card, lease, share or managed aircraft, and what it guarantees on a peak day, is basic logistical literacy.

articles.title: Seoul's twin fairs drew more than 150,000 people and produced no record breaking sale, which is precisely the argument their organisers are making
articles.body:
The fifth Frieze Seoul closed on Sunday after four days at Coex, drawing more than 70,000 visitors from 54 countries and regions, its most internationally varied audience to date, alongside 178 museum and institutional representatives from 25 countries, another record. Kiaf Seoul, the homegrown fair running in parallel for its twenty fifth edition, brought together 175 galleries from 18 countries and attracted about 80,000 visitors, some 8,000 of them on the closing Sunday alone.

The top reported transaction at Frieze was Kukje Gallery's sale of a 1971 painting by the Korean modernist Yoo Young-kuk for between KRW 2.2 billion and KRW 2.5 billion, or roughly USD 1.63 million to USD 1.85 million, the highest price recorded for a Korean artist at the fair since it began in 2022. Thaddaeus Ropac placed a 2026 Adrian Ghenie for EUR 1.1 million. At Kiaf, Gallery Hyundai reported more than USD 2.3 million from five works by Kim Tschang-yeul and three by Lee Seung-taek.

Neither fair produced the kind of headline deal that marked Frieze Seoul's 2022 debut, and the organisers were explicit that this is not the measure they use. Frieze's chief executive told a press conference during the fair that the market's strength is read in the total volume of transactions across price categories rather than in one or two large sales. Dealers described a Korean collector base with deep knowledge of Western artists and undiminished buying power, and newer galleries reported brisk sales of emerging artists at prices accessible to first time buyers.

The shift beneath the figures is generational. Kiaf's newly appointed creative director attributed the widening base to buyers less inclined to treat art as an investment, choosing artists to their own taste rather than following the blue chip names their parents collected. Frieze, which has seen a younger profile among fairgoers across Asia, will launch a Korean language edition of its magazine next year and has expanded its regional teams and institutional partnerships to hold that audience between fairs.
articles.why: Collections are increasingly assembled by younger family members buying to taste across many price points, which means more works arriving more often, and more handling, documentation, storage and installation passing through the household.

articles.title: A small house opens on the square at Meursault, offering Burgundy without the chateau
articles.body:
Maison Le Chevreuil has opened at 1 Place de la Republique, on the main square of the village of Meursault in the Cote de Beaune. The stated intention was to create a smaller, design led alternative to the grand chateau stays that dominate accommodation in Burgundy, in a region where the wine list is frequently the reason for the journey and the house is only the base.

Two local architects, Aubin Prost and Johanna Leserre, took on the renovation and the interiors. The reception does triple duty as check in desk, coffee counter and cocktail bar, with terrazzo floors made from fragments of local Corton stone, a rammed earth bar, natural clay plaster walls and oak detailing. Bedrooms have Hastens beds, rounded seating and curved showers whose shape is drawn from wine tanks.

The interest for a household is the type rather than the property. Small owner led houses in wine villages sit closer to a private visit than a hotel stay does, which suits a principal travelling to see growers, and they require more arrangement rather than less: appointments at domaines are made person to person, the good ones are booked months ahead, and the house itself will not do it.
articles.why: Wine country travel is arranged, not booked. The value a concierge adds is the introduction to the grower and the timing of the visit, and a small village address makes both easier to build a day around.

briefs.b: New York's fair returns to the Javits Center with roughly 230 galleries from more than 30 countries, having moved to late September this year. The Presents and Solo sections, for emerging galleries and single artist presentations, have each expanded by about 20 per cent, and the curated Platform and Focus sections are devoted to artists working across the Caribbean and to first generation North American artists shaped by the Caribbean diaspora.

briefs.t: 81,900, and the real count comes next year
briefs.b: HMRC figures for the final year of the non domiciled regime show the number of claimants, including those deemed domiciled, fell from 83,100 to 81,900, a drop of about 1 per cent. Around 9,000 left in the 2024 to 2025 tax year against 11,200 the year before, while new arrivals fell from 10,000 to about 8,600. The group paid GBP 9.7 billion in income, employment and capital gains taxes, up 9 per cent and the highest total in records going back to 2008. The government says it will only be able to estimate departures since the change accurately next year.

briefs.t: New duties for British households that employ
briefs.b: Key provisions of the Employment Rights Act came into force on 6 April 2026, making statutory sick pay a day one right for all workers and granting day one entitlement to paternity leave and unpaid parental leave. The main National Minimum Wage rate for workers aged 21 and over rose to GBP 12.71 an hour from 1 April, and a new Fair Work Agency began operating on 7 April as a single enforcement body for minimum wage, holiday pay and sick pay. Private households employing staff directly sit inside all of it.

Knight Frank's National Country Department completed GBP 173 million of prime country house sales in the first quarter of 2026, across 36 transactions at an average guide price of GBP 4.8 million. Eight sales exceeded GBP 5 million and three were priced above GBP 10 million. The firm nonetheless expects average prices across the prime country market, covering rural and urban locations outside London above GBP 750,000, to fall 2.5 per cent across 2026.

strap: A daily dispatch from the world you are entering

lead.title: Two roles the market cannot supply, and the households that want them are being told to start looking six months out
lead.standfirst: The domestic couple and the estate manager have become the hardest appointments in private service, and the recruitment calendar has lengthened to match.
lead.body:
Morgan & Mallet International has published its annual account of what private households actually ask for, drawn from a database of more than 50,300 candidates and from placements made across the United States, the United Kingdom, Europe and the Middle East between January 2024 and October 2025. The report is usually read for its salary tables. The more instructive passage this year is the one on scarcity, because it names two roles that money alone is not producing.

The first is the domestic couple. In France, 21 per cent of the agency's clients over the past year asked for one and could not find it. The arithmetic explains the shortage better than the pay does. A couple must be two competent professionals who happen to be in a relationship, willing to live in, willing to be hired and dismissed as a single unit, and willing to accept that a disagreement at home is now a staffing matter. The pool is small by definition and it does not grow in response to demand.

The second is the estate manager, which now accounts for 10 per cent of all requests the agency receives from the United States and sits inside the top five American roles alongside the chief of staff. Half of every estate manager brief the firm handles originates in America, where multi property ownership has become the norm rather than the exception. Most estate managers placed run at least three properties at once. The candidates are rare because the specification has quietly become three jobs in one: security judgement, technical literacy across the systems a modern house now runs on, and the management of staff and contractors who each think their own trade should come first.

Pay has moved to meet the shortage without closing it. An American estate manager is placed at between USD 150,000 and USD 250,000, a Swiss one at between CHF 110,000 and CHF 150,000, a British one at between GBP 75,000 and GBP 120,000. A domestic couple reaches USD 250,000 in the United States and CHF 160,000 in Switzerland, while the same couple in France is offered between EUR 45,000 and EUR 60,000. The agency records a further premium of 15 to 20 per cent for staff working under confidentiality agreements, and notes that 77 per cent of the personal assistant roles it fills in Los Angeles now require one.

The practical consequence is a change to the calendar. Households are advised to begin recruiting four to six months before they need someone, rather than the two to three months that was standard, and to budget 15 to 20 per cent above the published band for specialists. Average tenure in private service has fallen from roughly twenty years to about three, so the same house may run the exercise several times in a decade. Requests are forecast to rise by 12 to 18 per cent in the American and Emirati markets.
lead.why: Scarcity is the strongest argument a candidate has. Anyone who can present the estate manager's combination of security, systems and staff supervision, or who can offer a couple's two sets of hands under a single contract, is negotiating in the thinnest part of the market.
lead.src: Morgan & Mallet International, Household Staff Annual Report 2025/26

articles.title: Italy raises the price of its flat tax by half, and the households it was written for keep arriving anyway
articles.body:
Italy's 2026 Budget Law, Law 199/2025, lifted the annual flat tax paid by individuals who move their tax residence to the country from EUR 200,000 to EUR 300,000 with effect from 1 January 2026. The regime, introduced by the 2017 Budget Law, allows a new Italian resident to leave foreign income outside the ordinary income tax base and settle it instead with a single substitute payment, due in one instalment by 30 June, or by 30 July with a surcharge of 0.4 per cent.

The conditions are narrow and worth knowing precisely, because they shape who actually turns up. The applicant must not have been tax resident in Italy in at least nine of the ten preceding tax periods. The option runs for fifteen years and can be revoked. Family members can be brought under the same umbrella at EUR 50,000 each. Capital gains on the disposal of qualified shareholdings are excluded during the first five years. Holders are also exempt from Italian taxes on the value of property owned abroad and on foreign financial accounts, and gift and inheritance tax applies only to assets situated in Italy.

A 50 per cent increase in the entry price would, in most markets, be read as a deterrent. It has not been read that way here. The sums involved are trivially small against the fortunes they shelter, and the surrounding proposition has strengthened rather than weakened: an inheritance framework that remains gentle by European standards, access to the single market, and a city, Milan, that has been assembling the advisers, banks and family office infrastructure that a relocating household needs within walking distance of each other.

For anyone in service, a flat tax move is not an abstraction. It means a principal establishing genuine residence rather than a holiday pattern, which in turn means a house that must be run to a standard all year, a payroll registered in Italy, staff hired locally or relocated, and a family that will be counting days. It also means Milan, Lake Como and the Tuscan hills are absorbing households that used to be run from London.
articles.why: Tax regimes decide where households physically sit, and therefore where the jobs are. A private service career planned around London alone is now planned around a shrinking share of the European market.

articles.title: Transactions in prime London rise while prices keep falling, and the buyers are arguing rather than walking away
articles.body:
Knight Frank reported this week that the number of transactions across prime central London and prime outer London in the three months to August ran 2 per cent above the five year average. In prime central London alone, sales over the same three months were 6 per cent higher than in 2025. After several years in which the top of the London market was described almost entirely in the language of departure, activity has quietly returned.

Prices have not followed. Average values in prime central London fell 3.3 per cent in the year to August and are 23 per cent lower than they were eleven years ago. Prime outer London slipped 0.4 per cent over the year and is down 7 per cent across the decade. In sterling terms, and before inflation is considered at all, the most expensive residential addresses in Britain have been a poor store of value for more than a decade.

The agency's explanation for the divergence is behavioural. Stuart Bailey, who leads prime central London sales, said the difference this year is that buyers are using "pre-Budget speculation and bond market jitters to negotiate" rather than abandoning transactions altogether. Uncertainty has stopped being a reason to leave the table and become a tool for use at it. Underlying confidence, on this reading, is intact, and parts of the market are being bought because they look cheap.

What that produces on the ground is a change of ownership rather than a change of use. Houses in Belgravia, Knightsbridge and Holland Park are transferring at negotiated prices to buyers who intend to occupy them, frequently from overseas, frequently while keeping principal residences elsewhere. Each of those transactions ends with a property that needs opening, staffing, insuring, maintained through long absences and made ready at short notice.
articles.why: A falling price index and a rising transaction count point in the same direction for staff. Every completed sale is a household forming, and a household forming is a hiring event.
articles.src: Knight Frank, via Estate Agent Today

articles.title: Half a billion dollars of second hand yachts is tied up in Cannes this week, and the pre-owned market is where the season now begins
articles.body:
The Cannes Yachting Festival runs from 8 to 13 September across the Vieux Port and the enlarged Port Canto, with more than 700 boats, some 680 exhibitors and around 150 world premieres. It is the largest boat show in Europe and the event that opens the autumn yachting calendar, three weeks ahead of Monaco.

The number that matters to anyone working in this world is not the count of premieres but the brokerage fleet: more than 45 vessels above 25 metres, carrying a combined asking value of roughly half a billion dollars. That is a substantial quantity of existing tonnage assembled in one harbour, and it reflects where demand has settled. Yards are quoting long build slots, so an owner who wants a boat for next summer buys one that already floats.

The size profile has stopped climbing. Average length at this year's edition sits just below last year's figure and gross tonnage has shrunk slightly, a stabilisation after several seasons of steady growth in both. Cannes has always been the show where the direct relationship between owner, broker and yard does the work, and the density of large second hand boats this year is what makes matching supply to demand possible in a matter of days rather than months.

A pre-owned sale differs from a new build in a way that is felt below decks. There is no long fit out during which a crew can be assembled at leisure. A boat that changes hands in September may need a full interior team, a chief stewardess and a chef before the winter Caribbean season, hired against a handover date rather than a launch date.
articles.why: The brokerage market sets the hiring rhythm at sea. A yacht bought second hand needs its crew in weeks, which is why interior candidates who can join at short notice are the ones brokers keep on file.

articles.title: Champagne picked its earliest harvest in recorded history this year, and the cellar a household is buying for will hold less of 2026 than of anything before it
articles.body:
France recorded its hottest day since measurements began on 24 June 2026, when the national average temperature reached 30 degrees, beating the 29.4 degrees set in July 2019. Individual towns passed 43 degrees. It was the most severe of three heatwaves to cross the country between May and July, and the cumulative effect was to compress the growing season and pull picking forward by a week to a fortnight across almost every major appellation.

In Champagne, picking was expected to begin around 15 August, with the warm slopes of Montgueux potentially starting on 10 August. That eclipses the previous record of 17 August, set in 2020, and stands against an earliest documented harvest of 20 August 1822. Spring frosts had already cut early buds by roughly 40 per cent across the region, with losses ranging from 25 per cent in the least affected areas to 85 per cent in the Aisne. The Comite Champagne responded by capping the 2026 yield at 8,800 kilogrammes per hectare, equivalent to about 250 million bottles, against global shipments of 266 million bottles in 2025. Actual crop volume is expected to fall around 10 per cent year on year.

Bordeaux ran hot enough that merchants reached for 2003 as a comparison. Ground temperatures in some vineyards approached 50 degrees and estimates point to yield reductions of 20 per cent or more, with the main harvest brought forward to mid August against a September norm. In Burgundy, where picking was pencilled in for around 20 August, the concern was different. Laurent Delaunay, chairman of the Bourgogne wine board, said the region's "biggest concern isn't the heat itself, but the lack of water". Italy and Spain entered the summer with stronger reserves and report better fruit condition, and in Penedes the sparkling producer Juve & Camps began picking on 27 July, the first July start in more than a century of trading, using night harvesting to protect acidity in transport.

What none of this settles is quality, which will not be knowable until the fruit is in the cellar. What it does settle is volume. Less 2026 will exist, in the three French regions a serious cellar is most likely to be built around, than of the vintages either side of it.
articles.why: Cellar management is a household responsibility, and allocations are argued for months before bottles are released. Knowing which vintages are short, and why, is the difference between placing an order and being told there is none.

articles.title: The country that creates the most wealth scores 62.3 for holding on to it, and its own citizens are Henley's largest source of applications
articles.body:
Henley & Partners rebuilt its Private Wealth Migration Report this year around a Global Wealth Mobility Framework that scores jurisdictions across twelve dimensions and thirty eight weighted indicators, from tax treatment and rule of law to family inclusion and geopolitical resilience. The result is a ranking of structural competitiveness rather than of headline inflows, and the most striking entry in it is the United States, which scores 62.3.

The paradox is deliberate. America remains the largest engine of wealth creation on earth and is simultaneously the firm's biggest single source market for residence and citizenship planning. Applications from American nationals doubled in 2025 against the previous year and have stayed elevated through 2026. Only 7 per cent of those applications come from Americans already living abroad, meaning the demand is overwhelmingly domestic. Close to half is directed at European programmes and more than a quarter at Latin America and the Caribbean. Citizenship based taxation, fiscal complexity and slow immigration processing are the reasons given.

At the top of the framework sit Singapore at 79.5 and New Zealand at 75.8, followed by the Cayman Islands at 74.3, Cyprus at 73.5, the Netherlands at 72.8, Portugal at 72.5, Italy at 72.3 and Bermuda at 72.0. Italy's placing is credited to its flat tax regime, its inheritance framework and the emergence of Milan as an international financial and family office centre. Germany at 69.7, Norway at 69.0, the United Kingdom at 68.3 and France at 65.7 are classed as competitive jurisdictions under pressure.

The behaviour underneath the scores is what changes the work. In the first five months of 2026 the firm received applications from 86 nationalities across 47 programmes, and more than 28 per cent of applicants already live outside their country of nationality. Basil Mohr-Elzeki, who heads private clients for the Americas, describes clients who "increasingly think like portfolio managers", holding residence in one country, citizenship in another and structures in a third. Households of that shape do not relocate once. They maintain several bases simultaneously.
articles.why: A principal assembling a portfolio of jurisdictions needs someone who can keep three or four houses in a state of readiness across time zones, and who understands that day counting is a compliance matter before it is a scheduling one.
articles.src: Henley & Partners, Private Wealth Migration Report 2026

briefs.b: Business jets flew 1.95 million departures worldwide in the first half of 2026, up 4 per cent on the same period last year. Aircraft management operators, who fly on behalf of private owners, accounted for 423,300 of them, or 21.7 per cent of all activity, though that segment grew only 1.9 per cent. North America was up 5.0 per cent and Latin America 4.6 per cent, while the Middle East fell 17.8 per cent.

briefs.t: The Gulf hedges rather than leaves
briefs.b: The United Arab Emirates scored 85.3 in Henley's new framework, among the highest of any jurisdiction, on tax, investor access, family inclusion and connectivity. Enquiries from UAE based individuals nonetheless rose 41 per cent between the fourth quarter of 2025 and the first quarter of 2026, with applications for alternative residence or citizenship up 29 per cent. The firm reads this as contingency planning by expatriate families using the Emirates as a base, not departure from it.

briefs.t: Swiss watches level at half time
briefs.b: Swiss watch exports reached CHF 12.8 billion in the first half of 2026, down 0.7 per cent on the same period last year, with wristwatches at CHF 12.2 billion, down 0.6 per cent. June alone rose 11.2 per cent to nearly CHF 2.4 billion, a second consecutive month of rapid recovery after two years of decline.
briefs.src: Federation of the Swiss Watch Industry

briefs.b: Booking data from Haute Retreats shows Mediterranean villa demand for 2026 shifting towards larger, multigenerational stays of longer duration, with the Caribbean, Italy, Mexico and the French Alps taking the volume for summer and the festive season. Staff, and a private chef in particular, are among the most requested elements of the booking rather than an extra arranged afterwards.

strap: A daily dispatch from the world you are entering

lead.title: Thirty thousand pupils have left Britain's independent schools, and the places still being filled belong to families who never checked the invoice
lead.standfirst: The 2026 census shows a sector contracting almost everywhere except at the top, where the best known schools report record application volumes.
lead.body:
The Independent Schools Council census puts the number of pupils in British independent schools at just over 526,000, spread across 1,455 member schools, a fall of 3.5 per cent on the previous year and the lowest total in almost a decade. Some 30,000 pupils have left the sector since VAT of 20 per cent was applied to fees in January 2025, a figure already approaching the government's own long run estimate of 37,000. This is the first year in which the effect can be read at the start of an academic year rather than mid term.

The losses are concentrated at the points of entry. Year 12, the start of sixth form, fell 6.6 per cent, the sharpest single drop, as families moved children to state grammar schools, sixth form colleges and academies. Year 1 fell by the same margin and Year 3, the intake year for most preparatory schools, by 6.2 per cent. Year 7, the first year of secondary, was 5.6 per cent lower. Preparatory and primary settings fell around 5 per cent overall against 3.3 per cent for secondaries up to GCSE, with the largest regional declines in Scotland, Wales and the north east of England. Julie Robinson, chief executive of the ISC, said the figures represent "families facing difficult financial decisions".

The consolidation that follows is already visible in the ownership register. Cognita has shed more than a third of its United Kingdom footprint, selling twelve sites to Blenheim Schools and two to Redshift Education, while Chatsworth Schools has passed five campuses to Outcomes First Group. Mid market regional day schools, which depend on double income professional families sensitive to a sudden fee rise, are the ones cutting bursaries, narrowing curricula and postponing capital works, which in turn erodes the case for paying at all.

At the other end nothing has moved. Eton, Harrow, Winchester, St Paul's and Wycombe Abbey have held their numbers through the same period, several of them reporting record application volumes, because their intake is drawn from ultra high net worth domestic families and from overseas, for whom a 20 per cent increase changes the price but not the decision. Reporting on the same census also records a double digit fall in pupils with overseas parents and a steeper drop in new international entrants, which suggests the softening is happening below the tier one names rather than within them. A tax written to reduce exclusivity is producing a smaller and considerably more exclusive sector.
lead.why: The education file is one of the heaviest a private household carries: term dates that dictate the travel calendar, guardianship arrangements, boarding logistics, exeat weekends and the relationship with a school office. As families concentrate in a shorter list of institutions, that file becomes more standardised and more scrutinised.

articles.title: A private chef in an American house can now earn USD 300,000, and the kitchen has become the most contested appointment in the household
articles.body:
Private chefs working for American households now earn between USD 100,000 and USD 300,000 a year, according to a report from the household staffing agency Morgan & Mallet International. The ceiling has moved because the brief has changed: families who once booked the restaurant now want the person who cooks in it, at home, without a reservation, a photograph or a dining room of strangers. Chefs with Michelin experience are being recruited directly out of professional kitchens, and the best of them are, in the agency's phrase, able to name their price.

The rest of the house has moved with it. Household managers in the United States are quoted at between USD 150,000 and USD 250,000, and butlers as high as USD 180,000. What has risen fastest is not the base figure but the premium for proven experience, since the constraint in this market is not the number of candidates but the number who have already run a comparable house and can be referenced.

The less flattering figure in the same research is tenure. The average stay with one employer is now around three years, against a profession that once measured service in decades. Households are buying scarce people in a competitive market, and those people are being approached continuously once they are placed. Salary inflation and turnover are the same phenomenon seen from two ends.

For the chef specifically, the money buys something broader than cooking. The post carries provisioning across several residences, dietary and allergen protocols for family and guests, service that must be judged against restaurants the principals know well, and the ability to travel with the family and produce the same standard in an unfamiliar kitchen. It is a logistics role that happens to involve food, and it is priced accordingly.
articles.why: Pay in private service tracks scarcity and proven discretion, not qualifications. Knowing where the ceilings sit, and what a household is actually buying at that level, is the difference between negotiating a package and accepting one.

articles.title: Nine postcodes now carry USD 44 billion of California's last resort fire risk, and almost all of them are addresses that come with staff
articles.body:
The California FAIR Plan, created in 1968 as the cover of last resort for homeowners no private insurer would take, has become the first port of call for owners of multimillion dollar houses in fire exposed enclaves. The number of its residential policies rose 151 per cent between September 2022 and March 2026, and the risk it carries jumped 234 per cent to USD 700 billion. Nine zip codes out of more than 1,700 in the state now account for roughly 7 per cent of that liability, or USD 44 billion, a 135 per cent increase since 2022, according to a Bloomberg analysis of the latest data.

The concentration is unmistakably at the top of the market. Well off communities make up five of the ten highest liability zip codes. A single Lake Tahoe zip code, where about half the dwellings are second homes, carries USD 9 billion of risk. Lake Arrowhead, where roughly 60 per cent of dwellings are second homes, carries USD 7 billion. In Calabasas exposure rose 46 per cent between 2024 and 2025, and in Orinda, in the Bay Area, it rose 142 per cent to USD 5.6 billion.

The cost is socialised. Because the plan is funded by the state's insurers, who may pass certain expenses to their customers, part of the bill for insuring the largest houses is borne by everyone else. After the 2025 Los Angeles firestorms, FAIR faced a potential USD 3 billion liability in Pacific Palisades alone; regulators authorised it to collect USD 1 billion from insurers and allowed them to recoup half of that by adding between USD 11 and USD 176 a year to every policy in the state for two years. A University of California, Berkeley study in March concluded that the plan's exposure is disproportionately tied to higher income, high asset communities, with the premium burden falling more heavily on middle income households.

The practical position for a household is narrower than the headlines suggest. FAIR must accept any homeowner shut out of the private market, but it covers fire only, so a separate policy is needed for everything else, and payouts are capped at USD 3 million, which is a fraction of the rebuild cost of the houses driving the exposure. Brokers in Aspen, Vail and Telluride report policies being rebuilt across several carriers at many times the previous premium, and one proposal now under discussion would push second homes out of the plan altogether and into the lightly regulated surplus lines market.
articles.why: Insurability has become an operational matter rather than a paperwork one. The person running the estate holds the inventory, the valuations, the defensible space works, the vendor records and the evacuation plan, and increasingly it is that file, not the address, that determines what cover can be bought.

articles.title: Rotation has locked up the best interior crew at sea, and the yachts that need a chief stewardess are having to grow their own
articles.body:
The 2026 benchmarks published by the Antibes agency YPI CREW put a chief stewardess on a yacht of 30 to 40 metres at between EUR 4,000 and EUR 6,500 a month, rising to between EUR 7,500 and EUR 10,000 on 80 to 100 metres and above EUR 8,500 beyond that. A purser on 60 to 80 metres is quoted at EUR 7,000 to EUR 8,500, and above 100 metres at more than EUR 8,500, in both cases on equal rotation. A junior stewardess with under a year of experience starts at EUR 3,000 to EUR 3,500 with 60 to 90 days of leave.

The structural point sits underneath those tables. Rotational contracts are now standard on yachts above 60 metres, and a large share of experienced senior interior crew are committed to them, which means they are not on the market at all. Owners looking for a chief stewardess or head of service are therefore competing for a pool that has effectively been withdrawn, and the agency's advice is blunt: promote from within and invest in the people already aboard.

At the entry level the problem is the opposite. Interest in junior stewardess roles keeps rising, driven by television and social media, and candidates without a service background frequently leave within their first season, defeated by the hours, the constant proximity and the standard expected from the first day. Those who arrive from hotels or cruise ships adapt faster and stay longer, which is why genuine hospitality experience has become the differentiator at the bottom of the ladder as much as leadership is at the top.

The specialist bench keeps widening. Spa therapists, nurses, personal trainers, hairdressers and laundry masters are quoted at between EUR 3,500 and EUR 5,500 a month depending on vessel size, and demand for new wellness disciplines, reformer pilates among them, is growing across the larger fleet. The agency also notes that a good many departures recorded as wellbeing problems trace back to management gaps at head of department level, which makes leadership training for newly promoted crew the cheapest retention tool available.
articles.why: The interior of a large yacht runs on the same disciplines as a private house: service standards, housekeeping, provisioning, guest preferences and a small team living alongside the people it serves. A season at sea remains one of the fastest routes into senior land based positions, and the shortage is at exactly the rank most worth reaching.

articles.title: Christie's and Sotheby's have posted their strongest half in five years, and the category pulling new buyers in is the one a household already handles
articles.body: Christie's reported first half revenue of USD 4.5 billion, with public auction sales up 71 per cent year on year at USD 3.5 billion and a sell through rate of 91 per cent by lot. Sotheby's public auction sales came to USD 3.4 billion, up 59 per cent, with a sell through rate of 90 per cent and a record USD 826 million in private sales, taking total turnover to USD 4.4 billion, an all time high for the house. Both figures follow a difficult 2025 and were built on a handful of very large estates. The trophies did the heavy lifting. The collection of the publisher S.I. Newhouse totalled USD 630.8 million in New York in May and produced the two highest prices of the year so far, Jackson Pollock's Number 7A at USD 181.2 million and Constantin Brancusi's Danaide at USD 107.6 million. In London in June the Lewis collection made USD 406.2 million, the most valuable sale of Impressionist, Modern and contemporary art ever staged in Europe. Conservative estimates were the other lever: a Monet offered in New York at USD 6 million to USD 8 million sold for USD 19.6 million, while lots with pushed estimates drew thinner bidding. Behind twentieth and twenty first century art, the second largest category at both houses is now luxury, the catch all that covers watches, jewellery, cars, handbags, wine and memorabilia. Christie's luxury sales reached USD 539 million in the half, up 15 per cent, and its sale of the Jim Irsay collection of Americana made USD 105.2 million across five auctions. Watches in particular have moved: average bidder spend at Sotheby's is up around 60 per cent year on year at USD 129,000, with millennial and Gen Z buyers now roughly a third of watch bidders and demand shifting towards independent makers such as F.P. Journe and Rexhep Rexhepi. The houses treat that category as an entrance rather than a sideline. Christie's says 47 per cent of its new clients this year are millennial or Gen Z and that 85 per cent of its bids came online. Both are also lending against collections rather than waiting for them to be sold: Sotheby's completed a USD 900 million securitisation of art backed loans in January, the first to include loans secured against collectible cars, while Christie's reports clients borrowing against cars, handbags, watches and, increasingly, wine.
articles.why: Objects in the house are no longer only objects. They are catalogued assets, sometimes pledged as collateral, and their condition, provenance, storage and transport are handled by whoever runs the residence. Knowing which categories are moving, and why, is part of speaking the family's language.

briefs.t: London Design Festival opens on Saturday
briefs.b: The 24th edition of the festival runs from 12 to 20 September across the city's design districts, with installations, exhibitions, showroom openings and talks. It is the week when London's decorative trades, from furniture makers to lighting and textile houses, put their new work in public.

The historic racing meeting returns to the Sussex circuit for three days devoted to the period from 1948 to 1966, with period dress expected of spectators. It remains one of the fixed points of the British autumn calendar for collectors and their households.

Residential transactions in Dubai fell 31 per cent year on year in the second quarter to 34,850 deals, worth AED 84.9 billion, still the third highest second quarter on record. Sales above AED 15 million dropped 59 per cent to 578, while price per square foot kept rising across most communities, led by Palm Jumeirah Garden Homes at 37 per cent.

briefs.t: What a family office costs to run
briefs.b: J.P. Morgan's 2026 report, drawn from 333 single family offices across 30 countries, puts the average annual operating cost at USD 3 million, rising to USD 6.6 million for offices with more than USD 1 billion in assets. More than a quarter of that spending goes on outsourced services such as legal, trading and cybersecurity.

strap: A daily dispatch from the world you are entering

lead.title: Both chambers of Congress now hold a bill that would write 2.2 million domestic workers into the labour law everyone else already lives under
lead.standfirst: The National Domestic Workers Bill of Rights sits before the House and the Senate, and its provisions read like a description of how a well run private household already operates.
lead.body:
The Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 excluded domestic service from most of its protections, and the exclusion has never been fully undone. Live-in domestic employees working solely for private households remain exempt from federal overtime pay to this day. The National Domestic Workers Bill of Rights would end that. Representative Pramila Jayapal introduced the House version, H.R. 3971, on 12 June 2025 with 104 members of Congress behind it. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the Senate companion, S. 3396, on 9 December 2025, and it now sits with the Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions.

The bill amends both the Fair Labor Standards Act and the Civil Rights Act. It would extend overtime pay, paid sick days and the right to request time off for personal reasons. It would require meal and rest breaks. It would protect privacy, and it would bring domestic workers inside federal protections against workplace discrimination and harassment. It would also establish a national hotline through which workers could seek help on employment questions.

The drafting is unusually specific about paperwork, and that is the part worth reading closely. Employment would be subject to a written agreement. Where an employer and an employee agree to an on-duty meal or rest break, that too must be set down in writing, must be paid at the regular rate, and must be revocable by the employee in writing at any time. Where an employer wants to schedule work during hours the written agreement identifies as off-hours, or outside a good faith estimate of the schedule, prior written consent is required, and that consent may be given electronically.

The conditions the sponsors cite explain the emphasis. According to the House sponsor's office, the typical domestic worker in the United States earned USD 20,926 in 2023. Four in five receive no sick days. One in three receive no breaks during the working day. Those figures describe the sector as a whole, including cleaners paid by the hour across many houses, rather than the senior private household roles at the top of the market. But the legal exclusion applies to both, and the compliance burden of the bill would fall on the household that employs, not on the agency that placed.

Neither bill has moved out of committee, and prediction is not the point. The point is that the direction of travel is one way. Washington state's domestic workers law is already in force. California, New York and several other states have their own statutes. A private household that keeps written schedules, records hours, documents breaks and holds a signed employment agreement is not preparing for a bill that may or may not pass. It is simply operating the way most of the market is being pushed to operate.
lead.why: The professional standard is converging on the legal one. Written agreements, recorded hours and documented rest are becoming the mark of a competently run household, and a candidate who can build and maintain that paperwork is offering the principal protection as well as order.

articles.title: Spending on lived moments is outgrowing spending on objects by half again, and the money is moving towards the part of luxury a household actually arranges
articles.body:
The spring update of the Bain and Altagamma Luxury Goods Worldwide Market Study, published on 25 June, puts worldwide luxury spending at EUR 1,443 billion in 2025 and expects a range of EUR 1,440 billion to EUR 1,470 billion for 2026. Within that, personal luxury goods, meaning the handbags, watches, clothing and beauty that most people picture when they hear the word luxury, slipped to EUR 358 billion last year and is forecast to recover to between EUR 365 billion and EUR 373 billion this year, growth of 2 to 4 per cent. Bain assigns that base case a 70 per cent probability.

The more interesting number is not in the goods column. Consumer sentiment towards experiences is outgrowing tangible goods by 1.5 times so far in 2026. Bain describes this as a structural and cultural shift from ownership towards lived moments, and the categories holding up best sit squarely inside the working life of a private household: luxury hospitality, private jets, yachts and cruises are all resilient, supported by premiumisation, strong backlogs and new customers entering the market. Fine dining and gourmet food benefit from what the study calls a less but better mindset.

The weaker categories are instructive for the opposite reason. Luxury cars are a drag amid the transition to electric vehicles. Fine wines and spirits face softer consumption as drinkers reduce frequency or move to alcohol-free alternatives. Design and furniture are slowing as post-pandemic order backlogs clear and property markets stay constrained. Fine art is returning to growth as investors rebalance. In watches, Bain reports that connoisseurship is overtaking hype, with collectors rewarding craftsmanship and rarity, a shift that is also feeding the resale market.

The experiential detail is the most operationally useful part of the study. Immersive bookings across dining, leisure and entertainment are up 30 per cent on last year, driven by bespoke, slow-travel formats rooted in local culture. Travel to destinations outside the traditional hotspots has grown 20 per cent, a pattern Bain labels Elsewhereism. Multi-generational travel is rising, and roughly half of Gen Z say their brand preferences were shaped by their parents. Meanwhile half of luxury shoppers now check the secondhand market before buying anything new, and half already use artificial intelligence somewhere in the purchase journey.

Read together, these lines describe a client whose money is moving from the shop into the diary. Slower itineraries, unfamiliar destinations, several generations travelling as one party, and a rising expectation that the experience will be specific rather than merely expensive. That is not a retail brief. It is a logistical one, and it lands on whoever runs the household calendar.
articles.why: The categories growing fastest are the ones a private household books, coordinates and supervises rather than the ones it simply buys. Depth in travel planning, private aviation, yacht charter and food and wine is where the demand is heading.

articles.title: The busiest summer ever recorded ends with a small weekly dip, and the number that matters is not the slowdown but the map
articles.body:
WINGX data reported at the end of August put the 2026 summer season at nearly 947,000 business jet departures between 1 June and 23 August, the busiest in the firm's data set. That is 2.3 per cent above the summer of 2025 and 35 per cent above the same stretch of 2019. In the last full week of that period, activity fell 2.4 per cent against the same week a year earlier, while year to date volumes remained 3.5 per cent ahead of 2025. A soft week after a record summer is unremarkable in itself.

The regional breakdown is not. North America accounted for more than 71 per cent of worldwide business jet activity and is running 4.8 per cent ahead of last year. Europe is up only 1.1 per cent year to date, and almost all of that growth comes from Italy and Spain. Strip those two markets out and the rest of the continent is flat. In the week in question, European activity contracted 0.5 per cent.

Beyond those two regions the picture fragments further. Activity outside Europe and North America grew 1.1 per cent in the week, but the composition of that growth is uneven: Africa rose 14.5 per cent and South America 8.9 per cent, while the Middle East fell 3.7 per cent and Asia fell 9.8 per cent. Four regions, four directions, in a single week.

For a household that moves between residences, this is a supply story rather than a statistic. Aircraft availability, crew positioning, charter pricing and last-minute options are all functions of how busy a given region is at a given moment. A family flying inside North America is operating in the densest and most competitive part of the market. A family whose calendar runs through Asia or the Gulf is working in thinner conditions, where a single cancellation is harder to replace and where lead times matter more.
articles.why: Anyone who books private aviation for a principal is negotiating inside a regional market, not a global one. Knowing which region is tight this month is the difference between a confirmed aircraft and an apology.

articles.title: Five hundred artisans occupy a Venetian island for one month, and the objects a household handles every day are given the staging usually reserved for art
articles.body:
The fourth Homo Faber Biennial opened on 1 September and runs to 30 September on San Giorgio Maggiore, in the grounds and buildings of the Fondazione Giorgio Cini. Presented by the Michelangelo Foundation and held under the high patronage of UNESCO, it brings together more than 700 objects made by more than 500 artisans from over 70 countries, arranged across 15 immersive installations under the title An Island of Light.

The artistic direction is by the British artist and designer Es Devlin, whose Library of Light installation drew close to 200,000 visitors to the Pinacoteca di Brera during Salone del Mobile in Milan in spring 2025. Her staging for Venice takes the Venetian lagoon as its organising idea, treating each craft artist as an island of skill within a wider archipelago, and manipulates light through water, mirrors and movement to move the visitor between workshops, tools, materials and finished pieces.

The programme is deliberately unglazed. Artisans work in front of visitors throughout the month. There are participatory workshops in Japanese crafts, including hand-carving a hanko wood stamp and kintsugi, the repair of broken ceramics with visible seams of lacquer and gold. Food and beverage across the site is run by a Venetian restaurant rather than a catering contractor. An accompanying app carries the story behind each object and lets visitors vote for their favourite pieces.

The exhibition also spills into the city. Homo Faber in Città at Casa Sanlorenzo hosts two shows, one on master artisans of Venice and the Veneto curated by Artemest, and another on craftspeople from Luxembourg curated by De Mains De Maîtres. Venetian workshops listed in the Homo Faber Guide open their doors to the public through September, with suggested itineraries published online.

For anyone whose work involves the care of objects, this is the most concentrated month of instruction available anywhere. Understanding how a piece of lacquer, glass, textile or marquetry was made is the beginning of knowing how it should be cleaned, moved, stored and repaired, and of knowing which damage is reversible and which is not.
articles.why: Cultural fluency in private service is practical before it is social. A house manager who has watched a craft being made handles the resulting object differently, and speaks about it accurately to insurers, restorers and the family.

articles.title: Since March, an American house bought in cash through a trust has come with a federal filing attached, and the names behind the structure go on it
articles.body:
The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network's Residential Real Estate Rule took effect on 1 March 2026. It requires a federal report on non-financed transfers of United States residential property where the buyer is a legal entity or a trust. Purchases financed by a regulated lender are generally outside the rule, as are transfers made directly to an individual. Covered property runs from one to four family homes to condominiums, cooperatives and certain unimproved land intended for residential use, and there is no minimum purchase price.

The reporting duty does not sit with the buyer. Unlike the Corporate Transparency Act, which put obligations on entities themselves, this rule places the filing on a professional in the closing process: the settlement agent, title agent, escrow agent or attorney handling the transaction. Only one report is required per transfer, and the parties may allocate responsibility between themselves by written agreement. The report is filed electronically after closing and covers the property, the seller, the buyer and the beneficial ownership of the purchasing entity or trust.

Trusts receive particular attention. Transfers into revocable and irrevocable trusts alike may be reportable where the purchase is non-financed and no exemption applies, and the filing must identify the trust as well as the individuals who exercise control over it or hold significant beneficial interests in it. Exemptions exist but are narrow: transfers by reason of death, divorce, court order or bankruptcy, and certain Section 1031 exchanges.

The practical consequence, as advisers warned before the rule bit, is a slower and more document-heavy closing. Structures that families built for estate planning, asset management or simple privacy now generate information requests at the point of purchase, and the timetable of a transaction has to absorb them. A house that once completed quietly in a fortnight now requires a set of names to be assembled first.

None of this is visible from inside the household, which is exactly why it matters. The person preparing a new residence for occupation is working to a completion date that is now partly determined by a federal filing, and the discretion that the family assumes surrounds the purchase is more limited than it was a year ago.
articles.why: Property timelines drive household timelines: staffing, deliveries, works and the family's first night in the house all hang off completion. Understanding why a closing has slowed is part of managing the move rather than reacting to it.

briefs.b: The Cannes Yachting Festival runs from today to 13 September across the Vieux Port and Port Canto. It is the largest in-water show in Europe and the first fixture of the autumn brokerage calendar, opening two weeks ahead of Monaco.

Burgundy has become the most traded region on the Liv-ex fine wine exchange for the first time since 2022. Domaine de la Romanee-Conti, Ramonet, Leflaive and d'Auvenay together accounted for about a third of Burgundy trade in July.

briefs.t: PAD London returns to Berkeley Square
briefs.b: The 18th edition of PAD London runs from 13 to 18 October in Mayfair, with 66 exhibitors from 15 countries showing collectible design and craft. It remains the most efficient single stop for a household building a picture of the design market.

The kingdom's foreign property ownership law came into force on 21 January 2026, allowing foreign individuals and foreign-owned entities to hold real estate subject to implementing regulations. Acquisitions must be recorded in the national real estate registry to take legal effect.
