lead.title: The United States and Switzerland set the top rate for 25 of the 28 household roles, and the map of private pay narrows to two countries
lead.standfirst: An agency salary report drawn from more than 50,300 candidates, updated last week, shows the ceiling of the profession concentrated in a very small number of markets.
lead.body:
The household staffing agency Morgan & Mallet has updated its annual salary report, drawn from a database of more than 50,300 candidates and from placements made across the United States, the United Kingdom, Europe and the Middle East between January 2024 and October 2025. Read as a map rather than as a table, it says something blunt about where a career in private service pays. Of the 28 roles the agency tracks, the United States holds the highest recorded salary for 17 of them and Switzerland for eight. Between them, two countries set the ceiling for 89 per cent of the profession.

The American figures are led by the two posts that sit closest to the principal. A private chef and a chief of staff both reach USD 300,000. Below them come the personal assistant, the estate manager, the executive assistant and the domestic couple, each recorded at up to USD 250,000, then the butler and the house manager at USD 180,000 and the housekeeper at USD 160,000. Switzerland's strength lies elsewhere, in the roles built around children and around the fabric of the house: the maternity nurse at CHF 155,000, the governess at CHF 130,000, and the nanny, the caregiver, the family cook and the private chauffeur all at CHF 120,000, close to USD 144,000 at the 2025 average rates the agency used to convert.

The three remaining roles are instructive precisely because they are exceptions. The United Arab Emirates leads the world in one post only, the travelling nanny, at AED 600,000 or about USD 163,200. The United Kingdom holds the top rate for the laundress at GBP 90,000. Monaco leads for the personal coach at EUR 130,000. Each is a specialism rather than a general market, and each reflects a particular way of living: constant movement in the Gulf, a surviving tradition of formal linen in Britain, a dense concentration of principals in the Principality who train at home.

France sits at the other end of the same table. Across most of the 28 roles the agency records a French band of EUR 45,000 to EUR 60,000, whether the post is butler, estate manager, governess or chief of staff. The same title, with the same duties, can therefore be worth four or five times more once it crosses a border. The agency also reports that average tenure in these households has fallen from around 20 years to roughly three, and that is the mechanism by which those gaps become visible: staff move, and moving reprices them.
lead.why: Two decisions shape a private service salary more than any qualification: which role, and which country. On this evidence the second now matters at least as much as the first, and it is the one a candidate can still choose.
lead.src: Morgan & Mallet, Household Staff Annual Report 2025/26

articles.title: The Swiss school year opens this week beside Lake Geneva and will move to Gstaad in January, and the households move with it
articles.body:
The autumn term at Institut Le Rosey begins in the first days of September at the Chateau du Rosey in Rolle, on the shore of Lake Geneva, and runs to the middle of December, closing with the school's Christmas celebration, to which parents are invited. In January the entire school moves to its winter campus at Chalet Rex in Gstaad and remains there until the middle of March. In April it returns to Rolle for a spring term that ends at the close of June with graduation. The school takes pupils from the age of 8 to 18 and boards all of them. There are no day places and no weekly boarding.

Entry to the older years is decided in rounds rather than continuously. Dossiers completed by 8 October 2026 receive a decision in early November. Those completed by 26 November 2026 are answered in the middle of December. A third session takes dossiers completed by 11 February 2027 and reports in early March. For younger candidates admission is rolling, but the school advises families to register between June and September of the year before entry, because each year group and each nationality carries a quota and the quotas fill during the year. Candidates are invited to spend a day on campus and to sit entrance tests in mathematics, in English or French, and in their mother tongue.

The school does not publish its fees. It states plainly that it accepts no donations and holds no endowment, and that fees are its sole source of finance, which is how it explains its independence. It awards between three and five partial scholarships a year, selected between September and December, and no full ones. The application for financial aid alone carries a fee of CHF 500, and applicants are expected to sit in the top 5 per cent of their age group academically while also contributing to sport, the arts or humanitarian work.

For a house, the significance is the calendar rather than the fees. A school that moves campus twice a year sets the rhythm of the family that follows it: a Swiss autumn, a mountain winter, a spring back beside the lake, a travel week in October and a graduation at the end of June. Houses are opened and closed around those dates, rotas are built on them, and the October and February decision sessions fall in the same weeks in which a household is otherwise planning its winter.
articles.why: In many households the school calendar, not the office diary, is the fixed point of the year. Knowing when the terms begin and where they take place is basic planning material for whoever runs the properties.

articles.title: Starlink doubles the price of its business aviation plans, and connectivity moves out of the technology budget and into the operating budget
articles.body:
SpaceX has restructured the pricing of its Starlink Business Aviation plans, and for two of them the effect is a straight doubling. The Aviation Regional 25GB plan moves from USD 2,000 a month to USD 4,000. The Aviation Global Unlimited plan moves from USD 10,000 a month to USD 20,000. A new middle tier, Aviation Regional Unlimited, arrives at USD 12,500 a month. Existing subscribers were moved automatically on to the new plans on their first billing cycle after 7 August.

The structure of the charge matters as much as its size. The subscription bills the same amount every cycle whatever the aircraft does, so it behaves less like fuel or an hourly engine programme and more like a fixed maintenance subscription. An aircraft flown 200 hours in a year and one flown 600 hours pay identically for connectivity. For a family aircraft that sits for long stretches between school terms and summer moves, that changes the shape of the annual budget rather than simply its total.

The wider shift, as the trade press covering the change puts it, is that connectivity has stopped being an optional upgrade and become part of the ownership equation. Passengers now expect the cabin to work as an office and as a screen, and judge it against what they have at home. Installation costs are examined closely at the point of purchase. Recurring subscriptions have historically escaped that scrutiny, and at these levels they will not continue to.
articles.why: Whoever assembles the household or flight department budget will be asked why a line has doubled. Being able to explain that the plan is priced by tier and not by hours flown is the difference between reporting a problem and understanding one.

articles.title: Abu Dhabi takes its first Frieze in November and opens its Guggenheim in December, and the Gulf acquires an art calendar of its own
articles.body:
Two dates at the end of this year turn Abu Dhabi into a fixture of the international art year. Frieze Abu Dhabi holds its inaugural edition from 19 to 22 November at Manarat Al Saadiyat, with Deutsche Bank as global lead partner. Three weeks later, on 11 December, the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi opens. Designed by Frank Gehry and first announced in 2006, the building runs to more than 800,000 square feet, of which roughly 125,000 square feet is exhibition space across 30 galleries.

They arrive at the end of a season of about 16 weeks that opened in Seoul in the first days of September and closes in Miami Beach in early December. Between those points sit the Armory Show in New York from 24 to 27 September, Frieze London and Frieze Masters in The Regent's Park from 14 to 18 October, and Art Basel Paris at the Grand Palais from 21 to 25 October with 211 exhibitors from 41 countries. Until now the Gulf has been a source of buyers for that circuit rather than a stop on it.

A permanent museum of that scale, paired with a fair carrying the Frieze name, changes the direction of travel. Collections held in Gulf houses have generally been shown, valued and sold elsewhere, with the specialists, registrars and shippers flying in for the occasion. An anchor institution and an annual fair create local reasons for that expertise to settle, and local dates around which a household's own art year can be organised.
articles.why: A principal who collects will expect the household to know when the fairs open, where works travel afterwards and who handles them in transit. From this winter, two of those dates sit in the Emirates.

articles.title: Foreign nationals are now barely half the applications leaving British addresses for a second residence, and the rest are British citizens
articles.body:
Henley & Partners' Private Wealth Migration Report 2026 records a change in who is leaving the United Kingdom. So far in 2026, foreign nationals account for 53 per cent of all applications the firm processes from British addresses, leaving British citizens as almost the whole of the remainder. The firm puts the equivalent British share at 8 per cent in 2018. Applications from UK addresses rose 15 per cent between 2024 and 2025, and the United Kingdom has moved from the firm's twentieth largest source market in 2018 to consistently among its five largest.

The report attributes the shift to a sequence of policy changes rather than to any single one: the abolition of the non domiciled regime, changes to inheritance tax treatment, the closure of the Tier 1 Investor Visa, and a broader climate of fiscal uncertainty. In the framework the report introduces this year, which scores jurisdictions out of 100 across 12 weighted dimensions and 38 indicators, the United Kingdom sits at 68.3 and is classed as a competitive jurisdiction under pressure, alongside Germany at 69.7, Norway at 69.0, South Korea at 66.2 and France at 65.7.

At the top of the same table are the United Arab Emirates at 85.3, Singapore at 79.5 and New Zealand at 75.8, followed by the Cayman Islands, Cyprus, the Netherlands, Portugal, Italy and Bermuda. Italy's position rests on its flat tax regime for new residents and its inheritance tax framework, with Milan increasingly functioning as a family office centre. Greece, at 70.5, has absorbed demand displaced by Spain's closure of its golden visa and Portugal's withdrawal of the property linked route. The report's own conclusion is that when a government closes a pathway, the demand does not disappear, it relocates.
articles.why: A household that changes its principal residence changes everything downstream: contracts, payroll, visas, and which house is staffed in which season. British households are now among the most likely in Europe to be planning that move.
articles.src: Henley & Partners, Private Wealth Migration Report 2026

briefs.t: The chef at the top of the table
briefs.b: The private chef is the best paid household role recorded in the United States, at up to USD 300,000, and the United Kingdom follows at up to GBP 200,000. The United States accounts for 35 per cent of the agency's global requests for chefs, ahead of the Middle East and of France and Monaco at 20 per cent each. In Los Angeles, 41 per cent of the chefs placed hold dual certification in nutrition and culinary arts.

Global business jet departures fell 2.4 per cent year on year in the week of 17 to 23 August, while activity for the year to date remains 3.5 per cent above 2025. North America accounts for more than 71 per cent of world activity and is 4.8 per cent ahead of last year. European activity is up only 1.1 per cent for the year, and flat once Italy and Spain are removed.

The Armory Show returns to the Javits Center in New York for its 32nd edition with around 230 galleries, adding a Caribbean focus and an after hours programme. Independent 20th Century runs on the same days, for the first time in Sotheby's Madison Avenue home in the former Breuer building, with 56 exhibitors and more than 130 artists.

The British Museum shows the Bayeux Tapestry from 10 September until July 2027, the first time in nearly 1,000 years that the 70 metre embroidery has left France. Tickets through to the end of the year are already sold out. It is the kind of fixture a principal will expect to be arranged rather than explained.

strap: A daily dispatch from the world you are entering

lead.title: The world adds almost two million millionaires in a year, and the ultra-wealthy tier is the one growing fastest
lead.standfirst: Capgemini counts 25.3 million high-net-worth individuals worldwide and about 250,000 at the ultra level, the segment that actually runs staffed houses.
lead.body:
The thirtieth edition of the Capgemini Research Institute's World Wealth Report puts global high-net-worth wealth at a record USD 98.3 trillion at the end of 2025, an increase of 8.7 per cent and the largest single-year rise since 2018. The population behind that figure grew by close to two million people, to 25.3 million individuals holding investable assets of USD 1 million or more. Strong equity markets and easing inflation did most of the work.

The more consequential number sits at the top of the pyramid. The ultra-high-net-worth population, those with USD 30 million or more, stood at roughly 250,000 individuals, a rise of 9.4 per cent year on year, which makes it the fastest growing wealth segment for the second consecutive year. Their wealth rose 9.7 per cent, outpacing the broader high-net-worth group. Concentration is unchanged in character and sharper in degree: the top 1 per cent of high-net-worth individuals now account for 34.8 per cent of all high-net-worth wealth.

The United States supplied the largest single share of the increase, adding 736,000 new millionaires in 2025, more than any other country, and lifting its high-net-worth population by 9.2 per cent to 8.7 million. That growth is the backdrop to almost every American hiring statistic in private service this year, from the concentration of household briefs in a handful of states to the length of the average search.

For anyone entering this profession the ultra tier is the only line that matters. It is the bracket in which a family holds several residences, moves between them on its own aircraft, keeps a boat and employs people to make all of it work. A 9.4 per cent annual increase in that population implies something in the order of 21,000 additional individuals in a single year. The count is of individuals rather than households, so the number of new employers is smaller than that, and not every household at this level employs a full team. The direction is not in doubt. Training pipelines, agency rosters and the supply of people with five years of verifiable service do not expand at 9.4 per cent a year.
lead.why: The ultra-wealthy tier is the employer base for private service, and it grew faster last year than the number of trained people available to serve it. That imbalance is what sits behind every salary figure and every unfilled post reported this season.
lead.src: Capgemini Research Institute, World Wealth Report 2026

articles.title: Family offices rebuild pay around keeping people, and more than half of them now run a long-term incentive plan
articles.body:
The talent strategy of the family office is shifting from recruitment to retention, and the shift is showing up in the structure of pay rather than only in its level. Trish Botoff, whose firm has benchmarked family office compensation for more than a decade, told Crain Currency that retention is "not an HR cost to be minimized but a competitive necessity". The reasoning is arithmetic. Most family offices now expect candidates to arrive with prior family office experience, which narrows an already small pool, intensifies competition for the people already inside the sector and raises the cost of every departure.

The pay premium that follows from that scarcity has proved durable. Botoff Consulting's annual Compensation and Talent Planning survey has tracked a persistent gap between the salary increases awarded by family offices and the national operating-company benchmarks published by WorldatWork. Family offices tend to pay larger annual increases, in part because they are small and are not answering to an operating budget in the way a corporate function must. Increases spiked during the pandemic years and have moderated since, as the market tilted back towards employers, but the structural premium has held.

What is changing is the design of the package. According to the firm's 2025 Compensation Premium Report, 51 per cent of family offices now use long-term incentive plans, with adoption markedly higher among offices managing larger sums. Where such plans exist, deferred incentive compensation is the most common structure, followed by carried interest and by co-investment opportunities offered with and without leverage. A newer instrument gives junior staff exposure to the family's own investments without the complication of a loan: a bonus of, say, USD 100,000 might be paid half in cash and half set aside to invest alongside the family.

This matters to the residence as well as to the investment floor. In most modern structures the estate and household team sits inside the same organisation as the family office, is benchmarked by the same consultants and increasingly inherits the same instruments. The house manager who is offered deferral, or a share of a co-investment, is being paid in the family office's currency. Reading that offer correctly, and knowing what it is worth against a straightforward salary elsewhere, is now part of the competence of the role.
articles.why: The private household increasingly shares a compensation architecture with the family office it sits beside. A candidate who understands deferral and co-investment can value an offer properly instead of comparing base salaries alone.

articles.title: The private cabin attendant settles near USD 150,000, and the contract day rate holds between USD 900 and USD 1,200
articles.body:
The 2026 market data for corporate cabin crew has consolidated around a clear set of numbers. Experienced contract flight attendants working large-cabin aircraft bill between USD 900 and USD 1,200 a day. Most fly 15 to 20 days a month, which produces roughly USD 90,000 to USD 175,000 a year before per diems and expenses, and without the benefits that come with a salaried post.

On the employed side the range is wider and the midpoint has risen. Full-time attendants in established flight departments have historically been quoted at USD 65,000 to USD 120,000 depending on the aircraft, the market and the demands of the operation. The broader 2026 benchmarks now place USD 150,000 as the midpoint for genuinely experienced professionals, with a ceiling above USD 300,000 in the right operation, and put the benchmark for lead flight attendants and cabin managers in the United States at around USD 190,000.

The structure of the job explains the spread. Safety qualification is the entry ticket and is not negotiable: an attendant on a private aircraft is the cabin's safety officer before anything else. What separates the top of the range from the bottom is everything that follows, which is service. Most operators provide paid recurrent training and uniforms, and salaried posts carry health cover. Fleet growth and the continuing expansion of business aviation activity keep demand ahead of the supply of people who hold both halves of the qualification.

For a student of private service the relevance is direct. A private cabin is a household in miniature: one family, a very small team, a fixed standard, no possibility of stepping out to fetch what was forgotten. The skills are the household's own, dietary knowledge, table and beverage service, packing, discretion, anticipation, compressed into a few hours at altitude. The route between the residence and the cabin runs in both directions, and the published aviation ladder gives a candidate a second market against which to price her own experience.
articles.why: The cabin of a private aircraft draws on the same competences as the private house and publishes its pay more openly. A candidate who can read both ladders negotiates from a stronger position.
articles.src: Crewblast, private jet flight attendant market data 2026

articles.title: Manhattan signs 24 luxury contracts in the last week of August, and the buying season restarts before the families come back
articles.body:
Twenty-four Manhattan homes asking USD 4 million or more went to contract in the week to 30 August, according to the weekly Olshan Realty report, up from 15 in the week before. The most expensive was a condominium at Central Park Tower, 217 West 57th Street, asking USD 20.5 million.

The month reads as a curve rather than a trend. Twenty-one contracts were signed in the week to 2 August, 18 in the week to 16 August and 15 in the week to 23 August, described at the time as a late summer slump, before the rebound to 24. Nothing about that pattern is unusual for a city whose luxury market empties in August and refills the moment the calendar turns. The point is where the line sits as the season opens, and it has opened up rather than down.

The wider picture for the year has been one of a narrowing new development pipeline, which pushes activity towards resales and towards the buildings that already exist. Central Park Tower, the Flatiron conversion and the Upper East Side townhouses that led August's weekly tallies are all finished product. A buyer signing now expects to close in the autumn.

That sequence is the one to watch from the service side. A city household is staffed against a completion date, not against a contract date, and the searches that fill those houses begin the moment the deal is signed. September to November is when Manhattan restaffs, which means the residence assembled for a family arriving at the turn of the year is being recruited for now, several months before anyone moves in.
articles.why: City households are staffed against completion dates. Contracts signed in the first weeks of September usually mean posts to be filled before the end of the year.

articles.title: Britain fixes its Budget for 28 October, and the households weighing a move now have eight weeks of planning season
articles.body:
The Chancellor, John Healey, confirmed on 31 July that the Autumn Budget will be delivered on Wednesday 28 October, alongside an economic and fiscal forecast from the Office for Budget Responsibility. It will be his first Budget in the post, and the first fiscal event of the current government.

A good deal is already on the statute book or announced. Agricultural Property Relief and Business Property Relief, the two reliefs that have historically allowed land and private companies to pass down largely outside inheritance tax, have been restricted. Unused pension funds come within the inheritance tax net from April 2027. Higher rates apply to rental and savings income. The scope of inheritance tax has been widened so that United Kingdom agricultural land is caught even where it is held through a non-United Kingdom entity. The reform of the domicile regime, which replaced a system that had shaped where internationally mobile families kept their main house for two centuries, is now working through its first full cycle.

What a fixed date produces is a planning season. Advisers to private clients treat the weeks before a Budget as the window in which decisions that were being deferred are either taken or abandoned: whether to sell a property, whether to move a trust, whether to change the country in which the family spends most of the year. Speculation about further measures aimed at wealth has been persistent through the summer, which sharpens rather than softens that effect.

The consequence inside the house is rarely discussed until it arrives. Relocation decisions taken in November are communicated to household staff in December and executed in the spring, and the people who run the residence are usually informed last and affected first. A house manager who knows the date of the Budget, and who understands that the questions being asked of the family's advisers this month have staffing consequences next year, is doing the job properly. Where a family does move, the burden of proving that the move is real, in days, in records and in receipts, falls on the household.
articles.why: Fiscal dates set the calendar of the private house. Relocation, property and staffing decisions cluster in the weeks around a Budget, and the household is where they are carried out.

briefs.b: Six houses hold their autumn Asian art sales in New York from 14 to 18 September: Bonhams, Christie's, Doyle, Freeman's, Heritage and Sotheby's. Christie's runs from 15 to 18 September at 20 Rockefeller Plaza, with the Alan Medaugh collection of Hiroshige prints, South Asian modern and contemporary art, and Chinese art from a private North American collection. Bonhams opens the week on 14 September at 111 West 57th Street.

Hagerty's final tally for the August motor car auctions on the Monterey peninsula came in at USD 755.6 million, a record and an increase of 73 per cent on the USD 432.8 million taken over the same days in 2025. The average car sold made USD 925,000, against USD 559,000 last year, which says more about the quality of what was consigned than about a general rise in values.

Business aviation logged close to 947,000 departures worldwide from 1 June to 23 August, making it the busiest summer season on record: 2.3 per cent above the summer of 2025 and 35 per cent above the same stretch in 2019. North America accounted for more than 71 per cent of global activity and ran 4.8 per cent ahead of last year.

The 2026 interior crew guides place a chief stewardess on a 30 to 40 metre yacht at USD 4,500 to USD 6,500 a month, rising to USD 8,000 to USD 12,000 and above on vessels of 60 metres and more. Charter programmes pay 15 to 25 per cent more in base salary and add tips on top. The shortage of experienced interior crew with strong references is the reason the range keeps moving.

strap: A daily dispatch from the world you are entering

lead.title: Holiday records become a criminal matter in the British private house, and the mileage rate rises to 55p
lead.standfirst: Three changes under the Employment Rights Act land squarely on the household that employs staff, and the person who keeps the diary is now the person who keeps the evidence.
lead.body:
Since 6 April 2026, an employer in the United Kingdom must keep records of the annual leave its staff take and of how their holiday pay was calculated. The records may be held in whatever form the employer finds practical, but they must reach back six years and must show the amount of holiday taken, any additional holiday taken, any unused entitlement carried into the next holiday period, and the calculation behind each payment. Stafftax, the domestic payroll specialist that administers pay for private employers across Britain, states the consequence plainly for its household clients: failure to maintain adequate records constitutes a criminal offence carrying an unlimited fine.

The obligation is drafted for employers in general, which means it falls with identical force on the family that employs one nanny and on the estate that employs fourteen people. There is no small employer exemption and no domestic exemption. A second change took effect on the same date and is felt weekly rather than annually: the maximum mileage rate rose from 45p to 55p. In houses where a driver, a housekeeper or a nanny uses a private car for the school run, the pharmacy, the airport and the errand list, that single figure alters the monthly reconciliation and any household expense policy written before April.

The third change arrives on 1 January 2027 and is the one likely to alter behaviour in the private house. From that date the qualifying period for an unfair dismissal claim falls from two years to six months, and the compensation cap is removed. A household that parts company with a housekeeper in month seven, without a documented and legally fair process behind it, will be exposed to an uncapped award. Stafftax advises private employers to introduce formal probation reviews and regular check-ins, which is guidance about paperwork as much as about kindness.

None of this is administered by the principal. In most houses the person who holds the rota, signs off leave, checks the mileage claims and files the contracts is the house manager, the estate manager or the principal's private assistant. It is that person's filing that will constitute the employer's defence if a claim is ever brought. A holiday tracker that was a convenience in 2025 is a statutory record in 2026, and a probation review that was a courtesy becomes, from January, a piece of legal protection.
lead.why: Record keeping in the British private house has moved from good practice to statutory obligation, and the staff member who administers leave, expenses and probation is the one standing between the employer and criminal liability. That is a competence worth naming in an interview.

articles.title: Nearly four in five family offices now have the next generation shaping strategy, and almost none think the structures are ready
articles.body:
Ocorian, which administers structures for family offices and private clients across more than thirty years of operation, surveyed 200 family members and senior family office executives in February 2026, representing families with combined wealth of USD 119.37 billion across 16 markets including the United Kingdom, Switzerland, the United States, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, Hong Kong, India, Mauritius and the Channel Islands. The headline finding is generational. Some 79 per cent report that younger family members are now actively involved in developing and reviewing investment strategy, and 97 per cent say the priorities of those younger members differ from those of the founders.

The divergence is specific rather than atmospheric. The next generation pushes for greater exposure to private markets, more interest in digital assets, a heavier weighting towards tangible assets including property and lifestyle holdings, and a higher tolerance for risk overall. Ginny Goh, Ocorian's Director of Private Clients in Singapore, notes that the differences extend beyond the portfolio to geopolitical outlook and even to the question of where the family office should be based.

Governance has not kept pace. One family office in eight reports no natural succession of wealth and leadership, and 98 per cent agree that more needs to be done to strengthen succession planning. The gap between a next generation that is already at the table and a structure that has not been redrawn to accommodate it is where friction accumulates: slower decisions, competing instructions and, eventually, a reordering of who holds authority.

For the private house, that reordering is not abstract. Where the family office sits determines which jurisdiction employs the staff, which payroll they sit on and which visa regime applies. Where the next generation chooses to live determines which properties are opened, staffed and run. A house manager who has taken instruction from a founder for a decade may find, without any announcement, that the operative voice belongs to someone thirty years younger with different expectations of speed, technology and formality.
articles.why: A generational shift inside the family office reaches the household through jurisdiction, payroll and instruction. Knowing who now holds authority, and adapting reporting to that person rather than to the founder, is part of the job.

articles.title: Tokyo new flats pass 142 million yen while resale prices post a seventy-fifth consecutive monthly rise, and the volumes fall away
articles.body:
New condominiums in Tokyo's 23 wards averaged 142.49 million yen in the first half of 2026, up 9.1 per cent on the year, according to the Real Estate Economic Institute. Across Greater Tokyo the average reached 101.35 million yen, up 13.1 per cent, the first time a half year average has exceeded 100 million yen. Supply came in at 7,989 units, a fall of 0.8 per cent and the fifth consecutive half yearly decline, with developers squeezed by competition for central land, higher construction costs and overtime rules that have lengthened build programmes since 2024.

The resale market tells a more precise story. In the 23 wards, the average contracted price reached 1,357,700 yen per square metre in July, up 2.7 per cent and the seventy-fifth consecutive monthly increase since May 2020. Volumes moved the other way: 1,509 contracts, down 17.2 per cent and the seventh consecutive monthly fall. Across Greater Tokyo, unsold stock has risen for five months to 47,151 units, and newly listed asking prices now run roughly 40 per cent above the prices buyers actually pay, against a gap of about 15 per cent a year earlier. The central market is not falling. It is thinning.

Two forces still support prices, and one is weakening. Constrained new supply pushes buyers into existing stock. Overseas demand remains strong, helped by a yen that has stayed weak against the major currencies, which keeps Tokyo cheap in dollar terms even as yen prices climb. Borrowing costs, however, are at their highest in three decades. The Bank of Japan raised its policy rate to around 1.0 per cent on 16 June 2026, the highest since 1995, held it in late July, and next meets on 17 and 18 September. That pressure falls hardest on domestic buyers with variable rate mortgages, which is consistent with volumes collapsing while prices per square metre hold.

One administrative change matters to any international family buying in Japan. Since April 2026, non residents must file a report for all residential property acquisitions under the Foreign Exchange and Foreign Trade Act, the previous exemption for residential purchases having been withdrawn. It is a reporting requirement rather than a restriction: there is still no bar on foreign nationals owning Japanese property. But it is one more filing to track, and in most houses that tracking belongs to whoever runs the property file.
articles.why: Tokyo is becoming a standing address for internationally mobile families rather than a curiosity, and the reporting duty introduced in April lands on whoever keeps the property and compliance file for the household.

articles.title: The brokerage market takes 4.05 billion euros in six months, and the boats that change hands are the ones that need a full crew
articles.body:
The global superyacht brokerage market recorded 4.05 billion euros of sales in the first half of 2026, according to BoatPro, the market intelligence platform of Boat International, which tracks more than 13,000 superyachts. A total of 281 yachts of at least 24 metres changed hands between January and June, 129 in the first quarter and 152 in the second, against 272 in the same period of 2025 and 225 in 2024. Value rose faster than volume: from 2.21 billion euros in the first half of 2024 to 3.61 billion last year and 4.05 billion now. The figures rest on each yacht's last known asking price, since completed transaction prices are generally confidential.

The growth sits almost entirely at the top. Sales of yachts between 50 and 70 metres rose 52.9 per cent year on year, from 17 transactions to 26. The 40 to 50 metre band grew 10 per cent, while the 30 to 40 metre band fell 6 per cent. Smaller yachts still account for the greatest number of transactions, but limited availability at that size is part of the explanation. The average asking value of a yacht sold in the half reached 14.4 million euros, against 13.28 million in 2025 and 9.83 million in 2024.

The individual sales set the scale. Feadship's 100.7 metre Moonrise, asking 325 million euros, was sold by Burgess in just under six months and stands as the largest brokerage transaction of the year. The 89 metre Amels Mirage, formerly Here Comes the Sun, carried an estimated asking value of 165 million euros. The 66.3 metre Hampshire was listed at 85 million euros and the 61 metre Jubilee at 73.5 million.

Every one of those hulls is a payroll. A 50 to 70 metre yacht carries a permanent crew that a 30 metre boat does not, with a chief stewardess, a chef, an engineer and a rotation to be administered, and it demands shoreside coordination between the captain, the family office and whoever runs the family's calendar. A market shifting decisively towards larger vessels is a market creating senior interior positions and creating more work for the person ashore who has to keep the boat, the houses and the aircraft in the same diary. The backdrop favours the Monaco Yacht Show, which opens at Port Hercule from 23 to 26 September: of the 116 yachts in BoatPro's preliminary fleet report, 71 are listed for sale.
articles.why: Growth concentrated in the 50 to 70 metre band means more permanent interior and galley posts, and more shoreside coordination between yacht, houses and aircraft. That coordination is the private concierge's core work.

articles.title: Geneva Watch Days opens tomorrow with 71 houses and no fairground, and the independents keep the first week of September
articles.body:
Geneva Watch Days runs from 2 to 6 September, its seventh and largest edition, with 71 watchmaking houses presenting across the city. The format remains deliberately decentralised: rather than renting stands in a hall, brands receive visitors in their own showrooms, hotel suites and workshops around Geneva, and the public is admitted, which separates the event from the trade only fairs that dominate the watch calendar in the spring.

The line up mixes scale with independence. Established names including Breitling, Bulgari, Zenith, Oris, Doxa and Girard-Perregaux show alongside independent manufacturers such as MB and F, De Bethune, Laurent Ferrier, Urwerk, Greubel Forsey, MING and Konstantin Chaykin. Two central venues anchor the week: the Pavilion, and the Blue Box, which this year gathers more than 130 watches around the themes of Water, Earth, Air and Fire. A Collectors' Lounge runs on invitation.

The event was created in 2020 by eight brands, Breitling, Bvlgari, De Bethune, Girard-Perregaux, H. Moser and Cie., MB and F, Ulysse Nardin and Urwerk, at a moment when the traditional fair calendar had collapsed. Six years later it has become the fixture that opens the autumn, and the reason a certain kind of collector is in Geneva in the first week of September rather than anywhere else.

For anyone serving a collecting household, the practical value is knowing what the week is and is not. It is not an auction and nothing is being sold under the hammer. It is the moment new references are shown to the people who buy them, which means it drives the diary, the travel and, in the months that follow, the insurance schedules and the vault movements.
articles.why: Cultural fluency in watches is a working skill in a collecting house: knowing why a principal is in Geneva in the first week of September, and what arrives in the safe afterwards, is part of running the calendar.

articles.title: Europe picks its earliest harvest on record, and the 2026 cellar will be smaller in almost every French appellation
articles.body:
Three heatwaves between May and July compressed the growing season across nearly every major European appellation and pulled picking forward by a week to a fortnight. France recorded its hottest day since records began on 24 June 2026, when the national average temperature reached 30 degrees Celsius, beating the 29.4 degrees set in July 2019, with individual towns passing 43 degrees. The consequence that matters to a cellar is not the temperature but the volume.

Champagne expected to begin picking around 15 August, with warm sites such as Montgueux potentially starting on 10 August. That eclipses the previous record of 17 August, set in 2020, and approaches the region's earliest documented harvest of 20 August 1822. Spring frosts had already cut early buds by around 40 per cent across the region, with losses ranging from 25 per cent in the least affected areas to 85 per cent in the Aisne. The Comite Champagne has capped the 2026 yield at 8,800 kilograms per hectare, roughly 250 million bottles, the tightest cap since 2020 and set against global Champagne shipments of 266 million bottles in 2025.

Bordeaux is running hot enough that merchants are reaching for 2003 as a comparison. Ground temperatures in some vineyards have approached 50 degrees, and industry estimates point to yield reductions of 20 per cent or more, with the main harvest brought forward from the historical September norm. Not every parcel is under equal stress: Sylvie Cazes, owner of Chateau Chauvin and president of Saint-Emilion Grand Cru Classe, reports that blue clay parcels retained deep water reserves from a wet winter, and expects smaller yields of concentrated fruit. Burgundy pencilled its harvest for around 20 August against a traditional early to mid September start, where Laurent Delaunay, chairman of the Bourgogne wine board, says the concern is water rather than heat.

Italy and Spain entered the summer with stronger water reserves and currently report better fruit condition. In Catalonia, the Penedes sparkling house Juve and Camps began picking on 27 July at its Espiells estate, the first July start in more than a century of operation, and introduced night harvesting to keep fruit cool in transport. Quality across the vintage remains genuinely undecided and will be settled by rainfall in the final weeks. Volume is not: there will be less 2026 wine, and allocations of the wines that families actually drink and give will tighten accordingly.
articles.why: Allocations, forward purchasing decisions and cellar planning all follow from vintage size. A house that understands why 2026 will be short can secure what the family drinks before the shortage reaches the merchant list.

briefs.b: The Monaco Yacht Show returns to Port Hercule from 23 to 26 September. More than 120 superyachts are shown afloat, accompanied by around sixty tenders, with over 560 exhibitors across design, construction, brokerage and service. Roughly forty new launches are unveiled each year.

The 24th London Design Festival runs from 12 to 20 September across eleven design districts. The Global Design Forum sits at the V and A from 12 to 14 September, the London Design Medals are awarded on 14 September, and Shoreditch Design Week follows from 15 to 20 September with more than 60 showrooms and galleries taking part.

briefs.t: 86 per cent use it, 7 per cent buy it
briefs.b: Ocorian's global study of 200 family offices found 86 per cent already using artificial intelligence to improve operations and data insight, while only 7 per cent are currently seeking investment opportunities in the sector. Nearly three quarters expect to increase such investment within three years, and 72 per cent believe the real operational impact is two to five years away.

briefs.t: Fine wine still a quarter below its peak
briefs.b: The Knight Frank Luxury Investment Index closed 2025 down 0.4 per cent, a year of stabilisation after two years of losses, and is up 38.6 per cent over the decade. Within it the Liv-ex Fine Wine 100 fell 2.5 per cent in 2025 and sits almost 25 per cent below its 2022 peak, with Tuscan wines the most resilient category.
