lead.title: HMRC counts the non-doms and finds 73,400 of them, a fall of 0.5 per cent in the final year of the regime
lead.standfirst: The departure of Britain's non-domiciled residents, forecast for two years as a flood, arrives in the official statistics as a trickle.
lead.body:
For two years the London private household market has been managed on an assumption. The abolition of the non-domiciled tax regime, announced by one government and enacted by the next, was expected to empty Mayfair, Knightsbridge and Kensington of the families who employ butlers, house managers, private chefs and nannies. Agencies briefed candidates to expect relocations to Milan, Dubai and Geneva. Some households told staff their positions might not survive the move. The newly published HM Revenue & Customs statistics on non-UK domiciled taxpayers describe something considerably less dramatic.

Around 73,400 individuals claimed non-domiciled status in the tax year covered, a fall of roughly 400 people, or 0.5 per cent, on the year before. That is the entire measured contraction. Beneath the headline number the flows are quieter still: some 8,600 newly arrived non-domiciled taxpayers were recorded, down from about 10,000, while around 9,000 left the population, down from about 11,200. Fewer people arrived, and fewer people left. The gate did not swing open. It narrowed at both ends.

The revenue moved in the opposite direction to the narrative. Tax and National Insurance liabilities attributable to this group rose 9 per cent to GBP 13.6 billion, with income tax accounting for close to three quarters of the total and reaching its highest level since the tax year ending 2017. A smaller population paid materially more. This is the pattern that had already been suggested by academic work at the London School of Economics, which found that the very wealthy rarely relocate for tax alone, and by the Financial Times, which reported last year that the official departure figures were running in line with or below the Treasury's own forecasts.

The figures matter to anyone who serves a household in Britain because employment in private service is a function of residency, not of sentiment. A family that keeps a principal residence in London keeps a payroll in London. It keeps a house manager, a housekeeping team, a driver, a cook and, in the larger houses, a nursery. The alternative scenario, in which several thousand principals dissolve their British establishments within eighteen months, would have produced a visible collapse in vacancies. It has not appeared in the agency data, and it does not appear here.

What the numbers do not settle is the shape of the next few years. The regime measured in these statistics has now been replaced by a residence-based system, and the behavioural response to the new rules will only become visible in returns filed well after 2026. Households are also restructuring rather than leaving outright: a second residence in Milan or Dubai, a reduced London staff, more travel between houses. That is a change in the texture of the work rather than its existence.
lead.why: Residency, not rhetoric, determines where private service jobs exist. A household that keeps a London address keeps a London payroll, and candidates weighing an offer in Britain should read the official statistics before they read the headlines.

articles.title: Prime values across thirty world cities rise 0.6 per cent in six months, and the trophy house stops behaving like an investment
articles.body:
Savills published its Prime Residential Index for the first half of 2026 on 19 August. Across the thirty cities it tracks, prime capital values rose 0.6 per cent in the six months to June, and prime rents rose 1.1 per cent. For a market that spent the decade to 2022 accustomed to annual movements in the high single digits, this is close to standstill. The firm's forecasters expect average prime capital growth of 1.3 per cent across the same thirty cities for the full year, with Lisbon expected to lead.

The flatness is not weakness so much as a change of function. Prime residential has become, in Savills' framing, an asset that preserves value and attracts capital rather than one that generates returns. Buyers are cautious, geopolitical conditions are unsettled, and supply at the very top remains structurally limited because the number of genuinely trophy houses in any given city is fixed. The result is a market in which very little trades, very little is built, and prices consequently move very little.

For the household, a flat market changes the calculus of holding property. When capital values rose fast, the running cost of a large house was a rounding error against the annual gain, and principals were relaxed about carrying full staff in a house occupied six weeks a year. When values move 0.6 per cent, the running cost becomes visible on the family office spreadsheet. Estate managers in London, New York and Hong Kong are already reporting closer scrutiny of the annual house budget: energy contracts renegotiated, seasonal staff replaced by rotating teams shared across two residences, maintenance moved from calendar-based to condition-based schedules.

Rents rising faster than capital values, 1.1 per cent against 0.6 per cent, points the same way. Some families who would previously have bought a fourth or fifth residence are now renting it for the season instead. A rented house is a different management problem from an owned one: shorter lead times, an inventory and schedule of condition to police, a landlord's agent to manage, and a staff who must be brought in, trained on an unfamiliar building and stood down within months.
articles.why: A flat prime market pushes the running cost of a house into view. The person who can present a defensible household budget, and cut it without visibly cutting service, becomes considerably harder to replace.

articles.title: The private search now starts six months before the start date, and the qualification matters more than the length of the service
articles.body:
The traditional rhythm of private household recruitment assumed a two to three month search. A principal decided in March that the house needed a manager by June, the agency ran a shortlist in April, and the successful candidate served a notice period and arrived on time. Agency guidance published this year advises families to plan four to six months ahead instead. The change is small in words and substantial in practice: it means the household that begins looking in September is hiring for the spring, not for Christmas.

Two pressures produce the longer runway. The first is simple arithmetic. The population able to employ full household staff has grown faster than the population trained to work in one, and the strongest candidates are almost never on the open market. Agencies describe the good ones as passive: employed, comfortable, and moved only by a materially better proposition presented at the right moment. Reaching them takes time that a six week search does not contain.

The second pressure is a shift in what families are actually buying. Recruiters report that specialised qualification now outweighs raw tenure. A chef with a nutrition credential is preferred to a chef with twenty undifferentiated years. A nanny with a background in early years education, or in a STEM subject, is preferred to one with a longer but more general record. The most sought-after childcare candidates are hired for what they can teach, not simply for what they can supervise, and the market prices that accordingly. Graduates of the established British training colleges routinely open negotiations well above USD 100,000, and in Switzerland, the highest paying market for childcare, nannies and governesses are quoted around USD 144,000 and USD 156,000 respectively. A second language adds a documented premium of its own.

The practical consequence for anyone entering the profession is that the credential is now the entry ticket rather than the ornament. Time served still matters, and no family will hire an untested person to run a large estate, but the differentiating factor at interview has moved. Candidates who can name a specific competence, a language, a qualification, a technical discipline in wine, in security, in nutrition, in early years teaching, are being shortlisted ahead of longer but less legible careers.

The longer search cycle also changes how a candidate should manage her own calendar. If the best roles are being scoped four to six months in advance, the correspondence that produces a spring appointment happens in the autumn. Registering with agencies in the week one becomes available is, increasingly, registering a season late.
articles.why: The hiring calendar has moved before the salary did. Candidates who understand that the spring vacancies are scoped in the autumn, and who arrive with a nameable specialism, meet the market at the point where decisions are actually made.

articles.title: Auction sales at the three main houses reach USD 6.8 billion in six months, and London posts the sharpest recovery of any centre
articles.body:
After two indifferent years, the auction market has turned. Analysis by ArtTactic puts combined sales at Christie's, Sotheby's and Phillips at roughly USD 6.8 billion including fees for the first half of 2026, up about 70 per cent on the same period in 2025 and the strongest opening half since 2022. Christie's accounts for USD 3.4 billion, up from USD 2 billion. Sotheby's reaches USD 2.8 billion, up from USD 1.6 billion. Phillips posts USD 505.4 million, an increase of about 59 per cent.

The geography of the recovery is as notable as its scale. London sales rose 131 per cent to USD 1.42 billion, only fractionally short of the USD 1.47 billion recorded in the post-pandemic surge of 2022. That is a striking figure for a market that spent several seasons being described as structurally diminished, and it sits oddly alongside the persistent account of capital leaving Britain. The sell-through rate across the period reached about 91 per cent, supported by 131 white glove sales in which every lot found a buyer.

The growth is concentrated rather than broad. Trophy lots and the category the trade calls luxury collectibles carried the numbers. Sales of watches, design objects and memorabilia rose about 25 per cent, with memorabilia the standout at roughly USD 96.1 million, a rise of more than 300 per cent year on year. The middle market, the works between six figures and low seven, remains harder going. What has recovered is the very top and the collectable adjacent categories, not the market as a whole.

For a household, an auction rebound is an operational event before it is a cultural one. Objects bought at these levels arrive with obligations attached: condition reports, transit and installation, climate and light control, revised insurance schedules, updated inventories, and in many houses a security review. A single trophy purchase can change the specification of a room. The person who manages the house is usually the person who receives the crate, meets the installers, files the paperwork and remembers, three years later, where the certificate is kept.
articles.why: A buoyant auction season lands in the houses of the people who buy. Inventory discipline, condition records and insurance schedules are the quiet infrastructure that makes a collection possible, and they belong to the household, not the dealer.

articles.title: Europe flies 8,861 private departures in a mid-August week while America flies 30,707, and the summer's centre of gravity crosses the Atlantic
articles.body:
The private aviation figures for week 32 describe a European August that is thinner than usual. Europe recorded 8,861 fractional and charter departures, a decline of about 3 per cent against the same week last year, and about 12 per cent fewer than the preceding week. The national breakdown is uniform: the United Kingdom down 12 per cent on the week, France down 21 per cent, Italy down 19 per cent, and Germany down 16 per cent year on year.

The United States moved the other way. Fractional and charter departures there totalled 30,707, an increase of about 8 per cent year on year, led by double-digit growth in Florida, California and Texas. Europe, on Argus data, had already been essentially flat in June, up 0.1 per cent. The gap is not a European collapse so much as an American surge, and the most-cited explanation is the 2026 World Cup, which pulled a large volume of event-driven demand towards North America across the summer months. Fuel price volatility added a further drag on the European charter market, which entered the season more slowly than operators had forecast.

For anyone arranging movement on behalf of a family, the practical reading of these numbers is about availability rather than fashion. A softer European August means aircraft and crew are marginally easier to secure at Nice, Ibiza, Olbia and Mykonos than in the peak years, and that quoted rates have less scarcity built into them. The same week in the United States means the opposite: Florida, California and Texas repositioning is tight, crew duty limits bite, and a request made the day before is likely to be met with a repositioning charge or a refusal.

The operational discipline this rewards is the one that never changes. Confirm the aircraft type and tail number, not the category. Confirm the crew's duty window against the actual departure slot rather than the scheduled one. Confirm handling and ground transport at both ends in writing. In a tight market these are the details that fail, and they fail on the day.
articles.why: Charter availability is regional and seasonal, and the person who books the aircraft is the person who absorbs the consequences of a tight market. Reading the traffic data is the difference between a quote accepted and a movement that actually happens.

articles.title: Italy triples its flat tax to EUR 300,000 and Milan keeps arriving anyway, because the number was never the point
articles.body:
Italy's flat tax regime for new residents began in 2017 at EUR 100,000 a year on all foreign-source income. It doubled to EUR 200,000 in 2024. From January 2026 it stands at EUR 300,000. Individuals who transferred their tax residence before the latest increase took effect keep the EUR 200,000 rate for the remainder of their fifteen year window, a grandfathering provision worth EUR 100,000 a year to those who moved early.

A tripling of the headline levy in under a decade would, in most markets, be read as a deterrent. It has not been. Milan has continued to attract inbound wealth, and by most counts now sits third globally for inbound wealth migration and eleventh among the world's wealthiest cities, with roughly 115,000 resident millionaires and 17 billionaires. Estimates from Henley & Partners put the number of millionaires choosing Italy in 2025 at around 3,600. Those migration counts have been contested on methodological grounds, and should be treated as directional rather than precise, but the direction is consistent across sources.

The explanation is that a flat tax of EUR 300,000 is a small sum to the people it is designed to attract, and Italy is competing on something other than price. What Milan offers is a functioning European city with an international school system, direct connections, established private banking, a plausible cultural life and a legal environment that is comprehensible to a European family. Families reconsidering positions established elsewhere in the past decade, particularly in the Gulf, are weighing those attributes against a tax bill that, at these wealth levels, is a rounding error.

For the private service market this is a supply story. Every family that establishes an Italian residence establishes an Italian household, and Milan's pool of trained staff is shallower than London's or Geneva's. Agencies report demand for house managers, private chefs and drivers with Italian language competence and, crucially, with the ability to navigate Italian employment law, which is prescriptive on contracts, hours and dismissal in ways that catch out households accustomed to English or Swiss practice. A candidate with Italian, a European right to work and a working knowledge of the contratto collettivo for domestic employment is currently in a strong position.
articles.why: New residency hubs create new household establishments before they create a trained workforce. Italian language and a grasp of Italian employment law are, at this moment, among the most commercially useful things a candidate can hold.

briefs.b: The Morgan Stanley and WatchCharts secondary market index rose 1.5 per cent quarter on quarter in the second quarter of 2026, a fourth consecutive quarter above 1 per cent, though slower than the 2.5 per cent of the two preceding quarters. Patek Philippe led on value retention at 15.4 per cent, and Rolex's certified pre-owned programme cleared about USD 186 million. Twenty-seven of the thirty-five brands tracked were positive on the quarter.

Azimut Benetti heads Boat International's Global Order Book for the twenty-sixth consecutive year. Italian yards report sustained demand in the 35 to 80 metre band, and Southern Wind's order book now extends through 2028. For crew and shore-side staff, a full order book means delivery dates, and therefore recruitment windows, that are visible years in advance.

The General Aviation Manufacturers Association recorded 877 civil aircraft shipments worldwide in the first quarter of 2026, worth about USD 6.85 billion in billings. Business jet deliveries rose 14.9 per cent to 162 units and the value of aeroplane deliveries rose 19.1 per cent to USD 6.1 billion. The second quarter report is expected in late August.

Aggregated American job board data puts the average advertised pay for a private estate manager at about USD 89,401 a year as at June 2026, with most listings between USD 65,500 and USD 103,000. Packages at genuine ultra-high-net-worth level sit well above that range. The gap is a reminder that public salary averages describe the advertised market, not the private one, which is filled by referral and rarely posted at all.

strap: A daily dispatch from the world you are entering

lead.title: The domestic couple becomes the hardest hire in Europe, and the pay for the job has doubled in a decade
lead.standfirst: Requests for live-in couples across France, Switzerland and Monaco have risen by more than 60 per cent in three years, while the pool of people willing to do the work keeps getting older.
lead.body:
In 2026 a domestic couple working a villa, a château, a chalet or a large private estate in France, Switzerland, Monaco or Belgium is paid from 4,500 to 6,000 euros net a month for the two of them together. That figure sits on top of independent accommodation, generally on the property or immediately beside it, fully equipped and separate from the main house, and in most placements a service vehicle with fuel and maintenance covered. In Switzerland the equivalent package runs from CHF 120,000 to CHF 160,000 gross a year. In Monaco it runs from 80,000 to 115,000 euros gross.

Between 2015 and 2018 the same pairing was hired for from 3,000 to 3,500 euros net, accommodation included. Morgan & Mallet, which has recruited into private households since 2015 and reviewed the market in a January analysis updated in May, states plainly that this lower band has now disappeared from the professional market altogether. The doubling is not a spike. It is the result of demand that has outrun supply for a decade and shows no sign of correcting.

The demand side is measurable. Internal agency data shows an increase of more than 60 per cent in domestic couple requests across the French, Swiss and Monegasque markets in three years. In France, couples account for 21 per cent of top staffing requests, largely because a principal who houses one couple obtains two full-time workers for the cost of one set of accommodation. The turning point came between 2018 and 2022, when international owners arrived in Switzerland, Monaco and Belgium in numbers and brought with them stricter confidentiality requirements, higher presentation standards and properties full of technology that somebody has to understand.

The job description has moved with the money. A couple is now responsible for general surveillance of the property, interior and exterior maintenance, technical equipment, liaison with service providers, supervision of works, access control and the reception of owners and their guests. On wine estates, historic châteaux and mountain chalets the seasonal rhythm adds a further layer, because the property has to be readied before anyone announces they are coming. Owners increasingly expect a near managerial approach: not simply executing tasks, but understanding, alerting, planning and reporting back. That upgrade in expectation explains a large share of the salary increase.

The shortage underneath all this is demographic. The majority of genuinely operational couples placed in 2026 are over 40, with long experience in demanding environments. Younger candidates are deterred by the requirement of permanent presence, by the isolation of many properties and by a long-term commitment that sits badly against a preference for mobility. Junior profiles are rare and need substantial support before they reach the autonomy a UHNW owner assumes. As the current cohort approaches retirement, the gap widens rather than closes.

One quieter change deserves attention from anyone entering the profession. Because accommodation is tied to the employment contract and justified by the necessity of on-site presence, owners in all four markets are now drafting far more carefully: what the accommodation includes, what it does not, what the occupants may do inside it, and how quickly it must be released if the relationship ends. Contractual clarity has become the standard response to a market in which both the property and the people are worth a great deal more than they were.
lead.why: The couple is the only household role hired as a single unit, which makes the private life of two people part of the employer's operating risk and part of theirs. Anyone entering estate work should read the accommodation clause with the same attention as the salary line.

articles.title: The wealthy stop choosing a country and start assembling a portfolio of them, and the United States scores 62.3
articles.body:
Henley & Partners published the 2026 edition of its Private Wealth Migration Report on 16 June, and it is the most substantial rewrite since the series began in 2023. Where earlier editions counted millionaires crossing borders, this one introduces a Global Wealth Mobility Framework built with the analytics firm AlphaGeo, scoring jurisdictions across 12 dimensions and 38 weighted indicators covering tax treatment, rule of law, quality of life, investor pathways, family inclusion, geopolitical stability and capital mobility. Findings are benchmarked against World Bank, IMF, OECD and Global Peace Index data and cross-checked against the firm's own enquiry and application flows.

The scores rearrange the familiar map. The United Arab Emirates records 85.3, among the highest in the framework. Singapore follows at 79.5 and New Zealand at 75.8, the latter after reforms to its Active Investor Plus visa. A second cluster includes the Cayman Islands at 74.3, Cyprus at 73.5, the Netherlands at 72.8, Portugal at 72.5 and Italy at 72.3, where a flat tax regime for new residents and a favourable inheritance framework have helped push Milan towards being a genuine family office centre. Switzerland sits at 70.8, Greece at 70.5 and Monaco at 70.0.

The jurisdictions classified as competitive but under pressure make less comfortable reading for anyone whose employer keeps a house there. Germany scores 69.7, Norway 69.0, the United Kingdom 68.3, South Korea 66.2 and France 65.7. Applications from individuals with a British address rose 15 per cent between 2024 and 2025, and so far in 2026 British citizens account for almost half of all applications processed from UK addresses, against 8 per cent in 2018. Enquiries from German nationals rose 16 per cent between the fourth quarter of 2025 and the first of 2026, and France has climbed from the firm's top 40 source nationalities in 2024 to its top 15.

The United States is the paradox the report dwells on. It scores 62.3, well below its standing as the world's largest engine of wealth creation, and is simultaneously Henley's single largest source market. Applications from US nationals doubled in 2025 against the previous year and remain elevated. Only 7 per cent come from Americans living abroad, which means the demand is domestic. Nearly half of those applications are directed at European programmes and more than a quarter at Latin America and the Caribbean.

What is being bought is not relocation. In the first five months of 2026 the firm received applications from 86 nationalities across 47 investment migration programmes, and more than 28 per cent of applicants already lived outside their country of nationality. The pattern the report describes is a sovereign portfolio: residence in one jurisdiction, citizenship in another, business and banking structures in a third, so that no single government holds the whole of a family's life and capital. Even in the Emirates, where enquiries rose 41 per cent and applications for alternative residence 29 per cent between the fourth quarter of 2025 and the first of 2026, the reading is diversification rather than exodus.
articles.why: The household follows the jurisdiction. A family holding residence in one country and citizenship in another needs staff who can be moved legally and quickly, which is why portability of a passport and a work permit is now a hiring criterion as real as references.

articles.title: Alpine prices rise for a fifth straight year, and the chalet stops being a winter house
articles.body:
Knight Frank's Alpine Property Report 2026 records a market moving against the grain. While a number of global prime residential markets slowed, prime ski homes rose 23 per cent on average over the past five years, and the firm's Alpine Property Index gained 3.3 per cent over the last twelve months.

The gains are concentrated rather than general. Andermatt leads the index at 14.6 per cent, a rise attributed in large part to the loosening of restrictions on foreign ownership there. Davos, the second most expensive resort on the index and a place that fills with heads of state once a year, rose 10.5 per cent. Cortina d'Ampezzo added 10 per cent. St Moritz and Méribel each rose 7.1 per cent, and Gstaad 6.2 per cent.

The reason given is not snow. Kate Everett-Allen, who heads European residential research at Knight Frank, describes Alpine property as having evolved from seasonal playgrounds into year-round sanctuaries. Flexible working, a durable interest in permanent mountain living and a continued appetite for wellness and open country have turned six-week houses into twelve-month ones. Resorts have responded by investing in schools, infrastructure and services that only matter if people are there in June.

The practical consequence is a different kind of house. A property occupied all year needs continuous maintenance, a supply chain that functions in the off season, and someone in place to run it when the family is not there. That is a materially different staffing problem from opening a chalet for a fortnight at Christmas and closing it again in April, and it is arriving in the same valleys where qualified live-in couples are already scarce.
articles.why: Year-round Alpine living converts the seasonal caretaker into a permanent household with a permanent payroll. For anyone building an estate career, the mountain resorts are becoming full-time postings rather than winter contracts.

articles.title: A charter is confirmed on WhatsApp at three in the morning, and the broker is not in the conversation
articles.body:
EnterJet, a London firm that says it handles around 900 charters a month through a broker-free online process, completed its first booking made entirely through WhatsApp this summer. The company's founder, Charles Robinson, now 25, who entered the industry at 17 and set up the business in 2024, spent a year building the AI agent behind it, named Celeste, on the reasoning that clients will use a messaging application already on their telephone but resent downloading and repeatedly logging into another one.

The details of that first booking are worth reading closely. The request was made at three in the morning and the flight cost USD 13,000, which Robinson claims would have been from 5 to 10 per cent more through a traditional broker, who in any case might not have been awake. The whole exchange took 46 minutes, of which 43 were the client considering options. Once the client accepted, confirmation took under 90 seconds and the flight briefing arrived as a PDF in the same thread. Celeste responds to an opening brief in from 30 to 45 seconds, and pricing and availability are drawn from operator feeds in real time rather than composed by the model. A human team supervises and takes over anything requiring judgement.

The trade is not uniformly convinced. Matt Feldon of the boutique broker Smart Aviation uses AI in the running of the business but doubts clients want it in the conversation, arguing that chartering an aircraft is a personal act and that a model has no empathy. His firm keeps someone on call around the clock and confirms bookings in anything from 15 minutes to an hour, though he concedes that depends on an operator answering. James Farley, co-chief executive of Victor, put the objection more sharply: discretion is fundamental to private aviation, clients expect confidentiality around their travel, their preferences and their personal information, and any use of AI has to be controlled so that it never costs that trust. He notes that even clients who built AI companies themselves still value the human relationship.

The direction of travel is nonetheless clear. Elevate Jet, a US operator of thirty years' standing, launched its own agent, Ruby, earlier in 2026 inside an application that matches trip requests to aircraft with instant pricing. Robinson observes that nothing in the architecture prevents a client's own AI agent from negotiating with his, given an itinerary, an aircraft requirement and a budget, which would remove the human from both ends of the transaction. He says his firm is not doing that today, but calls it a reasonable place for this to go next.
articles.why: The value of whoever books the aircraft is shifting from finding the price to exercising judgement, holding confidences and knowing the unwritten preferences of the principal. Those are precisely the things an agent cannot read off an operator feed.

articles.title: Rotation becomes standard above sixty metres, and the senior interior crew a yacht wants are already committed elsewhere
articles.body:
The 2026 interior salary guide published by YPI CREW, the Antibes crew agency, sets out what the yacht side of private service now pays and, more usefully, what it now concedes. A purser on a yacht of from 60 to 80 metres earns from 7,000 to 8,500 euros a month on equal rotation, from 8,000 to 10,000 euros on 80 to 100 metres, and from 8,500 euros above 100 metres. A chief stewardess on a 30 to 40 metre yacht earns from 4,000 to 6,500 euros with 60 days of leave, rising to from 7,500 to 10,000 euros on equal rotation once the vessel passes 80 metres. A junior stewardess of under a year's experience earns from 3,000 to 3,500 euros at any size, with from 60 to 90 days of leave.

The structural fact behind those numbers is that rotational roles are now standard on yachts over 60 metres, and a significant share of experienced senior interior crew are locked into long-term rotational posts. They are, in the agency's blunt phrasing, simply not available. That closes one door and opens another: a capable stewardess with a few seasons behind her can now step into a chief stew or head of service appointment considerably earlier than she could have expected five years ago, provided the yacht is willing to develop her.

Recruitment at the entry level is a different story. Candidate volumes keep rising, driven partly by television and social media, and a large proportion of those candidates leave within their first season, unprepared for long hours, constant proximity to guests and colleagues and service standards that do not relax. Those arriving from hotels or cruise ships adapt faster and stay longer, which is why service sector experience has become the differentiator at the bottom of the ladder rather than certificates.

At the top of the ladder the agency makes an observation that applies equally on land. Across all seniority levels, communication, adaptability and discretion are rated as important as technical service skill, and many crew departures that present as wellbeing problems can be traced to gaps in management capability at head of department level. Leadership training for the newly promoted, proper reference checks and cultural alignment at the point of hire are described as the most effective levers for reducing turnover.

The last shift is in what an interior department contains. Demand keeps growing for spa therapists, nurses, hairdressers, beauticians, personal trainers and yoga and Pilates instructors across the larger fleet, with Reformer Pilates increasingly requested by owners and guests. A spa therapist with advanced training earns from 4,000 to 5,500 euros a month, a nurse from 4,000 to 5,000, and a laundry master above 100 metres from 4,000 to 5,000 on equal rotation. These are specialists who rotate roles frequently in order to keep their qualifications current, which makes professional development a retention tool rather than a benefit.
articles.why: A house and a yacht now compete for the same person, and land-based service experience travels well in that direction. The yacht's answer to burnout, which is leave written into the contract, is the benchmark against which private households are increasingly judged.

articles.title: Two casks from a distillery that no longer exists sell for GBP 4.25 million, and the buyer inherits the decisions still to be made
articles.body:
On 10 March 2026 at Christie's in London, two casks from the original Karuizawa distillery in Japan sold for a combined GBP 4,250,000, around USD 5.65 million. Each cask made GBP 2,125,000 including buyer's premium, and together they became the highest value lots ever sold by Christie's Wine and Spirits.

The provenance explains the price. The casks, numbered 6195 and 888, were distilled in 1999, the final year before the original Karuizawa distillery ceased production, and no more will be made. They were offered from the private collection of Sukhinder Singh of Elixir Distillers, one of the most closely watched names in rare spirits, and had been maturing in a Speyside warehouse.

What distinguishes a cask from a bottle is that it is unfinished. Each of these yields roughly 420 bottles, and the buyer now holds influence over how the whisky matures from here, when it is bottled and how it is eventually released. That is a set of decisions rather than an object, and decisions of that kind require storage, insurance, monitoring and, at some point, action.

The wider spirits market gives the result its edge. The category-wide expansion of the last decade has given way to a more selective market in which volumes are softer and collectors fewer, but in which rarity, strong age statements and unrepeatable provenance still command serious money. A distillery that closed a quarter of a century ago is, by definition, the one thing the market cannot make more of.
articles.why: Collections of this kind arrive in the household as administration, not as shopping. Knowing that a cask carries a maturation decision, a bonded warehouse and an insurance line is part of the cultural fluency the job now assumes.

briefs.t: One in ten, and hard to fill
briefs.b: In the United States, estate managers account for 10 per cent of all household staffing requests, yet very few candidates combine the technical, security and management experience the role now demands. Estate managers routinely run large teams and work alongside protection staff, a level of responsibility that rules out most applicants.

The United States and the United Arab Emirates are now the fiercest and best-paying markets for private staff, with UAE compensation expected to reach from USD 120,000 to USD 140,000 as demand grows. In the United Kingdom, restricted access to EU workers since Brexit has tightened the London pool and pushed salaries upwards.

The United Kingdom carries the highest demand for nannies of any market, close to a quarter of all placements worldwide. Nanny placements run at a 96 per cent success rate and successful candidates typically arrive with six years of experience, with first aid training treated as standard rather than a distinction.

Greece has emerged as one of the clearest beneficiaries of Europe's shifting investment migration landscape, scoring 70.5 on Henley's new competitiveness framework after Spain closed its golden visa and Portugal withdrew its real estate linked route. The lesson drawn is that when governments close established pathways, demand does not disappear, it relocates.

strap: A daily dispatch from the world you are entering

lead.title: The private kitchen starts paying restaurant money, and the chef who cooks for one family can now earn USD 300,000
lead.standfirst: A new household staffing report puts the top of the private chef market at USD 300,000 a year, and the reason is that the wealthiest families no longer want to be seen eating out.
lead.body:
The figure comes from the Beyond the Butler household staff industry report published this year by Morgan & Mallet International and taken up by CNBC in July. In the United States, a full-time private chef now earns between USD 100,000 and USD 300,000. The lower end covers a competent cook running a single household kitchen. The upper end is reserved for chefs with restaurant pedigree, and increasingly for chefs who have held a Michelin star, hired to reproduce that standard in a private dining room where nobody is watching.

The logic behind the number is not culinary vanity. It is privacy. A family that can afford any table in New York or London has discovered that the most exposed forty minutes of its week is the walk from the car to the restaurant door. Bringing the kitchen inside the house removes the photograph, the neighbouring table, the sommelier who recognises the face. The chef becomes an instrument of discretion as much as of gastronomy, which is precisely why the price has moved.

The report also prices the specialisms. Chefs trained in medically constrained cooking, coeliac-safe kitchens, severe allergy protocols, restricted sodium or renal diets, can effectively name their own figure, because the pool of people who can do that work to a high standard and hold their nerve in a private house is very small. The same report puts butlers as high as USD 180,000, a number that would have looked implausible five years ago.

For the household as a whole this is a structural shift rather than a salary story. The kitchen becomes the single most expensive line in the staffing budget, which means it also becomes the most scrutinised. A chef on USD 250,000 arrives with expectations attached: a proper equipment budget, a purchasing account, a second pair of hands for large covers, and a house manager who can plan menus around travel weeks rather than improvising on the morning.

It also changes who does the recruiting. Restaurant chefs do not read domestic staffing advertisements. They are approached, quietly, through agencies and through other chefs, and they are usually weighing the offer against a kitchen of their own. The household that wants one has to be able to describe the job as a career rather than a service, and that description is written by whoever runs the house.
lead.why: The chef is now the highest paid person in most private kitchens, and the person who manages the household budget, the purchasing and the travel calendar is the person who makes that hire work or fail.

articles.title: There are now roughly 8,030 single family offices in the world, and Deloitte expects 10,720 of them by 2030
articles.body:
Deloitte's Family Office Insights Series puts the current global count at about 8,030 single family offices, up from 6,130 in 2019, a rise of 31 per cent in six years. The projection is for roughly 9,030 next year and 10,720 by 2030, a 75 per cent expansion across the decade. Total wealth managed inside these structures stands at around USD 5.5 trillion today and is forecast to reach USD 9.5 trillion by 2030.

The geography matters more than the headline. North America holds about 3,180 of them, Asia Pacific 2,290 and Europe 2,020. The Middle East, with roughly 290, is small in absolute terms but is the fastest growing region from a low base. Hong Kong alone now counts 3,384 single family offices by Deloitte's local study, having added 681 in two years, a reminder that the definition varies by jurisdiction and that the numbers should be read as orders of magnitude rather than a census.

A single family office is not simply an investment desk. In practice it is the administrative spine of a family's entire life: the entity that pays the household payroll, holds the leases on the houses, insures the art, charters the aircraft and signs the confidentiality agreements. As the number of offices grows, so does the number of professionalised employers sitting between a principal and the staff who serve them.

That is the part that concerns anyone entering private service. Twenty years ago a house manager reported to the principal or the principal's spouse. Increasingly the reporting line runs to a chief of staff or a chief operating officer inside the family office, someone recruited out of banking or consultancy who expects budgets, service level standards and written handovers. Compensation research this year puts the base salary for a family office chief of staff at roughly USD 175,000 to USD 200,000, rising above USD 300,000 where the office manages more than USD 2 billion.

The practical consequence is that the household is being audited. Vendor contracts, overtime, staff turnover and property running costs are now line items that somebody reviews quarterly. The estate manager who can produce a clean set of figures and a defensible rationale for every supplier is in a very different position from one who cannot.
articles.why: The family office is becoming the employer of record for private staff, which means the household role is judged on documentation and cost control as well as on service.
articles.src: Deloitte Private, Family Office Insights Series

articles.title: Dubai sells 296 homes above USD 10 million in six months, and a single apartment goes for USD 114.9 million
articles.body:
Knight Frank's half year analysis records 296 residential sales above USD 10 million in Dubai between January and June, worth USD 5.1 billion in total. That is 14 per cent more by value than the first half of 2025, 16 per cent more by transaction count, and 49 per cent above the same period in 2024. The first quarter alone produced 165 such sales, the second 131, including a record 26 homes changing hands above USD 25 million.

The most expensive single purchase was a six bedroom apartment in the Aman Residences tower in Jumeirah Second, which sold for USD 114.9 million, or AED 422 million. Two later deals cited by the firm give a sense of the pace: a six bedroom villa on Jumeirah Bay Island at USD 76.3 million, and an 80,000 square foot plot on the Naia Island reclamation at USD 152.5 million.

By location, Dubai Hills Estate led with 51 sales above USD 10 million, just ahead of Palm Jumeirah on 50. Palm Jebel Ali, which is not due for completion until 2028, came third with 40. That a scheme still under construction ranks third in the ultra prime table tells you how much of this market is bought off plan and staffed years later.

Knight Frank is careful about the context. Most of these deals were agreed before the current period of regional uncertainty and register with a delay of four to six weeks, so the figures describe a market as it was rather than as it is. Prices across the mainstream market have eased by between 5 and 20 per cent depending on district, while prime neighbourhoods have held up better. The firm notes that only 4 per cent of homes were resold within twelve months last year, against 25 per cent in 2008, which is the clearest evidence that these are households moving in rather than speculators moving through.

For private service that last point is the whole story. Villa communities such as Dubai Hills and Al Barari are family districts with schools attached, and the rising school enrolment figures Knight Frank cites mean permanent residence. Each of those 296 houses is a staffing brief: a house manager, a driver, a nanny or governess, a chef, and a security arrangement, in a market where the supply of experienced English speaking household staff has never kept pace with the supply of houses.
articles.why: Every ultra prime sale in Dubai converts within a year or two into a household that has to be staffed, and the emirate is now creating those households faster than the region can train people to run them.

articles.title: Lürssen delivers the 114 metre Nausicaä, and the quietest thing aboard is the power plant
articles.body:
On 23 May Lürssen announced the delivery of Nausicaä, a 114.2 metre yacht built under the project name Cosmos and designed in its entirety, exterior and interior, by the Australian industrial designer Marc Newson. Single designer commissions at this scale are rare. So is the claim the yard makes about the result, that almost nothing changed between the concept presented six years ago and the vessel that left the shed.

The engineering is where the interest lies. The yacht runs a diesel electric plant of five engines driving fully electric azimuth pods, supported by a 2 MW battery bank large enough to carry every hotel load on board, climate control, lighting, galley, at peak, with no generator running. In practice that means extended periods at anchor in silence and with no local emissions, and the yard has configured the vessel to accept a methanol fuel cell system, which converts methanol into hydrogen to make electricity. The hull is certified Ice Class 1D, so the same boat is intended for polar work and for the tropics.

The interior breaks with convention in a way that will interest anyone who has run a household. There is no main deck saloon. Guests arrive into a two level atrium, and the main deck is given over entirely to an art gallery built around a central sculpture, with wall space left open for rotating works. Above it sit a circular balcony, a sushi bar and a table tennis area. At the top of the vessel a 56 square metre owner's study, the Skydome, is enclosed by seven hot bent glass panes, each 62 millimetres thick and weighing 1,050 kilogrammes, shaded by bronze shutters on a sliding circular rail.

Tender logistics have been engineered rather than improvised. A 12.5 metre sportsfish tender sits in a dry dock served by a sledge system rated to 16 tonnes, with tracks that extend over the swim platform into the water and then retract completely, leaving a teak lined recreational space that can be closed off by a hydraulic beam in following seas.

None of this is decoration for the crew. A yacht that carries a rotating art collection on its main deck needs humidity and light discipline and a condition record. A yacht that can lie silent at anchor for days changes the guest experience and the watch routine. And a tender system with a 16 tonne sledge is a piece of machinery with a maintenance schedule, not a toy.
articles.why: Yachts are becoming technical estates, and the shore side staff who coordinate guests, art, provisioning and refits need to understand the systems they are booking around.

articles.title: One anonymous collector sends more than 900 objects to Sotheby's, and the sale runs until 2027
articles.body:
Sotheby's has announced Magnum Opus, a multi part sale of more than 900 works from a single anonymous collector, carrying an aggregate estimate above USD 60 million. The material runs from antiquity to the twentieth century and is spread across 25 collecting categories, including paintings, jewellery, books and design. The first sales take place in New York from 21 to 23 October, after which the collection continues to be dispersed across Sotheby's New York and Paris rooms into 2027.

A Canaletto view of the Grand Canal looking east towards Santa Maria della Salute, estimated at USD 6 million to USD 8 million, leads the group. Degas, Picasso, Max Ernst and Fragonard are also represented. The interesting figure is not the top estimate but the arithmetic underneath it: 900 lots against USD 60 million gives an average of well under USD 100,000 per object, which describes a collector who bought widely and continuously rather than a handful of trophies.

That pattern is the one most private houses actually contain. A serious collection is rarely twenty famous pictures. It is hundreds of objects across a dozen categories, acquired over decades, with provenance files in varying states of repair, and it is usually the household rather than an art adviser that knows where any given piece physically is.

The sale also arrives after a strong London summer, where the three major houses combined for around USD 560 million, roughly three times the previous year, led by Sotheby's dispersal of works from the collection of Joe Lewis, which made nearly USD 393 million across 25 lots. Appetite at the top is not in doubt.

For anyone running an estate, a single owner sale of this size is a useful case study in what good record keeping is worth. Cataloguing 900 objects to auction standard requires photographs, measurements, condition notes, purchase invoices and export history. Households that maintain that inventory in life save their principals months of work, and considerably more than months when the collection eventually moves.
articles.why: Inventory, provenance files and condition records are household documents long before they are auction documents, and the person who keeps them is usually the estate manager.

briefs.b: Henley & Partners projects that about 165,000 millionaires will change country of residence in 2026, after a record 142,000 in 2025. The United Kingdom heads the outflow table for the first time in the decade the firm has tracked the data, while the United Arab Emirates remains the leading destination.

The three major auction houses took around USD 560 million between them in London this summer, roughly triple the previous year. Sotheby's sale of works from the Joe Lewis collection accounted for nearly USD 393 million across 25 lots, the largest single evening total ever recorded in Europe.

Global business aviation flight activity rose 5.6 per cent year on year in July, with departures 4.4 per cent above June. Turboprops led the annual expansion at 4.7 per cent, ahead of light jets at 4.2 per cent and midsize jets at 4.1 per cent.

Deloitte China counts 3,384 single family offices in Hong Kong, an increase of 681 in two years. The concentration underlines how quickly the Asian private wealth infrastructure, and the household staffing demand attached to it, is being built out.

lead.title: The 75th Pebble Beach Concours closes Monterey week, and the collector's centre of gravity moves towards cars built in his own lifetime
lead.standfirst: Five auction houses, a forecast approaching half a billion dollars and a quiet generational shift in what the wealthiest households now choose to collect.
lead.body:
Every August the Monterey Peninsula becomes the centre of the collector car world. Five major auction houses, Bonhams, Broad Arrow, Gooding Christie's, Mecum and RM Sotheby's, set up within a few miles of one another, and the week closes on the links at Pebble Beach with the Concours d'Elegance, which reached its 75th edition this year. Ahead of the week, analysts at Hagerty placed the midpoint of their sales forecast at roughly USD 470 million, with an optimistic scenario near USD 496 million. Either figure would put 2026 at or beyond the existing record of USD 471.2 million, set in 2022.

What matters more than the headline number is what produced it. Lot counts were expected to stay roughly flat, and the share of reserve lots to tick up only slightly. The change was in the mix. More seven and eight figure cars were consigned this year than at any previous Monterey, and a record 177 lots were forecast to sell above USD 1 million, against a previous high of 158 in 2022. Headline consignments included a Ferrari 250 P, a McLaren F1 GTR, several Ferrari Enzos, a Chevrolet Corvette Grand Sport and a Shelby Cobra Daytona Coupe, the last two absent from the auction block since 2009.

The generational point is the interesting one. Modern supercars, meaning cars built from the mid 1980s onwards, were projected to account for roughly 60 per cent of total sales. The average model year of cars on offer has moved from 1967 to 1974 in only three years. The prewar classics and Enzo-era Ferraris that once defined the top of the Monterey leaderboard are ceding ground to machines the buyer remembers from his own youth. Taste is following demographics, and it is doing so quickly.

The market underneath these results is not uniformly strong. Hagerty's broader Market Rating, a gauge of overall collector car health, has sat around 59.01 for close to a year, squarely in flat territory, while its longer-running Market Index is down 17 per cent from its December 2022 peak. Cars valued below roughly USD 250,000 have softened noticeably. The pattern industry watchers describe is K-shaped: trophy assets keep setting records while the broad middle treads water. For context, 2025 finished at USD 432.8 million, the second-highest total on record, but strip out a single USD 26 million charity Ferrari Daytona SP3 and the growth over 2024 was a modest 4 per cent.

Sell-through rate is the number the trade watches rather than the total. Last year roughly three quarters of lots found buyers across the major houses, with wide variation between them. A high proportion of cars failing to meet reserve, even alongside record headline sales, would indicate strain inside the luxury tier itself.
lead.why: A collection of this scale is an operational responsibility before it is an aesthetic one, and the household is what moves it, insures it, stores it and enters it. Knowing which era a principal collects, and why, is the difference between administering a garage and understanding a passion.
lead.src: Modern Car Collector, via Yahoo Finance

articles.title: Discretion stops being a virtue and becomes a line in the contract, worth 15 to 20 per cent on top of the salary
articles.body: The Morgan & Mallet Beyond the Butler 2025/26 report, examined by Spear's, records something the trade has long understood but rarely priced: confidentiality now carries a measurable premium. Roles carrying strict confidentiality obligations pay 15 to 20 per cent more than comparable positions without them. In Los Angeles, 77 per cent of personal assistant roles require a non-disclosure agreement. Some households impose a social media ban outright, and others ask staff to hand in their telephones on arrival. The lengths principals will go to are instructive. One Manhattan billionaire hired a butler who had never worked on the East Coast, specifically to avoid the overlapping social circles through which household detail travels. Certain very senior placements are conducted under such secrecy that the recruiter never learns the client's identity. The premium is not paid for silence in the abstract. It is paid for the absence of any route by which information could leave the house. The pay scales attached to this are no longer domestic in scale. The United States pays the most for 60 per cent of all household roles. Private chefs reach USD 300,000, executive assistants run from USD 120,000 to USD 250,000, and at the top of the household the chief of staff reaches USD 300,000 with the estate manager at USD 250,000. American principals expect round-the-clock support and staff who can hold both private and business responsibilities, which narrows the eligible pool considerably. There is a structural reason discretion has become expensive. Families are buying more properties in more countries, and each house adds people who see things. Average tenure across household roles now sits at about three years, and nannies typically stay two to three. Shorter tenures mean more former employees carrying more knowledge, which raises the value of the ones who can be trusted not to use it.
articles.why: Discretion is the one competency that cannot be demonstrated in an interview and cannot be recovered once lost. It is now written into the contract and reflected in the number, which means it will be assessed as rigorously as any technical skill.
articles.src: Spear's, on the Morgan & Mallet Beyond the Butler 2025/26 report

articles.title: Global wealth grows 10.8 per cent in a year, and the fastest expansion happens in the band that actually employs household staff
articles.body:
UBS published the 17th edition of its Global Wealth Report on 30 June, covering 56 markets that together hold more than 92 per cent of the world's wealth. Global personal wealth rose 10.8 per cent in USD terms during 2025, the fastest pace since 2017 and well ahead of the 4.6 per cent recorded in 2024. Growth was strongest in Europe, the Middle East and Africa at 17.5 per cent, followed by the Americas at 8.5 per cent and Asia-Pacific at 5.9 per cent. Currency movements, principally the weaker dollar, amplified gains outside the United States.

The number of USD millionaires rose 1.5 per cent, close to one million new millionaires, or more than 2,600 a day. The United States accounted for almost half of them, adding over 440,000. Switzerland remains the highest-ranked market for average wealth per adult at USD 910,382, ahead of the United States and Luxembourg. More than half of all global personal wealth still sits in the United States and mainland China combined.

The segment worth watching for anyone in private service is not the millionaire count but the tier above it. UBS records that growth was particularly strong in the bands from USD 5 million to USD 100 million, the group the report calls the bigger siblings of the everyday millionaire, and that this acceleration was most pronounced in mainland China, Australia and the United States. That band is precisely where a household stops being run by the family and starts being run by staff.

UBS also flags a divergence that complicates the headline. Since 2020, average wealth and median wealth have moved apart, and the report's own tables show the gap plainly: the United States ranks second on average wealth per adult at USD 696,277, yet its median sits at USD 68,998. Residential property remains the dominant asset for most households up to the everyday millionaire level, which limits participation in market-driven gains. Future outcomes, UBS concludes, will depend increasingly on access to investable assets and the ability to diversify.
articles.why: The USD 5 million to USD 100 million band is the growth engine of private staffing demand, and it behaves differently from the billionaire tier. These are first-generation employers who often have no household template, and who rely heavily on the professionalism of the first person they hire.

articles.title: The Hamptons runs out of houses, inventory falls to 1,166 and the summer season becomes a contest for what little exists
articles.body:
The East End's second quarter, analysed by Jonathan Miller of Miller Samuel, tells a story of demand meeting an empty shelf. There were 425 sales in the quarter, 12.3 per cent below the decade average, and sales have now fallen year on year for three consecutive quarters. Inventory dropped 9.5 per cent annually to 1,166 listings, 15.8 per cent below the ten-year average, with listings down in three of the past four quarters.

Prices moved in the opposite direction. The middle of the market, from USD 1 million to USD 5 million, took a record 67.8 per cent share of total sales, with median price rising 16.1 per cent annually to USD 2.2 million. Sales below USD 1 million fell to 14.6 per cent, close to a record low, while sales at USD 5 million and above reached a high of 17.9 per cent. Miller attributes much of this to a shift in the housing stock rather than pure price growth: builders on the East End are not putting up small houses, and the modest cottages that remain are being replaced by homes two or three times their size.

The top of the market behaved as it usually does. Bridgehampton, taken with Water Mill and Sagaponack, recorded the highest median at USD 5.33 million, up 12.2 per cent year on year, and took three of the seven sales above USD 20 million in the quarter. Amagansett saw sales fall 45 per cent and volume fall 16.4 per cent, yet still posted the second-highest median at close to USD 4.3 million. Hampton Bays remains the only submarket with a median below USD 1 million, and local agents expect that to change.

Judi Desiderio of William Raveis described a winter that was slow for both sales and rentals, followed by a second quarter in which activity built like a snowball. The pattern of the past several years holds: fewer trades each year, less inventory each year, and prices that keep climbing regardless.
articles.why: Scarce inventory means families hold houses longer and renovate rather than move, which lengthens the estate manager's horizon and shifts the role from transition management towards long-term stewardship of a single property.
articles.src: 27east, on Miller Samuel and William Raveis second quarter data

articles.title: The aircraft the wealthiest actually want is a single-engine turboprop with a two-year waiting list, and it is winning on ground time
articles.body:
The Pilatus PC-12 is not a jet. It is a Swiss-built single-engine turboprop, first unveiled in 1994, and it has become one of the most sought-after aircraft in private aviation. Some 2,200 have been delivered and they have flown more than 11 million hours. Pilatus now runs a two-year waiting list for new aircraft, and brokers report pre-owned examples selling for more than they cost new. Aircraft that fetched USD 6.4 million a few years ago now trade above USD 7 million, and rarely sit on the market for more than three months. The latest version, the PC-12 PRO, starts at USD 7.8 million.

The appeal is not speed or cabin size. It is the combination of a 290 knot cruise at up to 30,000 feet, a range of 2,070 miles, and the ability to use small airfields and grass strips that jets cannot. Jonathan Clough of Jetfly, whose firm owns, manages or operates 30 PC-12s, gives the arithmetic for a run from Surrey to Saint Tropez: by jet it is 45 minutes to Farnborough, 90 minutes in the air to Toulon-Hyeres and often 90 minutes by road, at least four hours end to end. By PC-12, it is 15 minutes to Fairoaks near Woking, two hours to La Mole, and 25 minutes to Saint Tropez, three hours in total. Handling fees at Farnborough run to GBP 1,500, and double at weekends. At Fairoaks and La Mole they are in the hundreds.

The cargo door is a quiet part of the appeal. Art collectors use the aircraft to move large works that no small jet can accommodate, and Jetfly cites one client who bought a PC-12 specifically because the door took his son's full-size powered wheelchair. James Banham of Oriens Aviation notes that the aircraft held around 80 per cent of its value after ten years before the pandemic, and rather more since.

The flight data supports the anecdote. WingX recorded roughly 333,500 PC-12 flights in the first half of 2026, up 4.3 per cent year on year. Commercial operators running private charter, air taxi and air ambulance work accounted for 41 per cent of flights and grew 7.5 per cent. Fractional operators took 8 per cent and grew 6.2 per cent. North America dominates with 72.8 per cent of flights, Europe holds 12.1 per cent. Charles Robinson of Enterjet reports a 46.3 per cent rise in PC-12 charter requests year on year, driven particularly by technology founders under 35. Around 100 aircraft will be built in 2026, against 84 of the predecessor NGX delivered in 2025.
articles.why: Door-to-door time, not aircraft category, is what the principal experiences. Whoever builds the itinerary should know which small airfields exist near the destination house, because the right strip can remove an hour of road from every trip.

articles.title: The five-star hotel discovers that the surest way to fill itself is to put a hundred years of Italian coachwork on the lawn
articles.body:
Luxury hotels have always parked something desirable by the door. What has changed is that several are now staging the events themselves. In Piazza della Repubblica, the Anantara Palazzo Naiadi hosted the inaugural Anantara Concorso Roma, gathering 66 exceptionally scarce Italian cars, a field valued at around GBP 350 million, and moving them under police escort down the Via Nazionale to the parkland of Villa Borghese. It was the first concours held in Rome since 1960, and it marked a century since the 1926 Concorso Romano delle Carrozzerie.

The programme ran three days: a rooftop reception for entrants and sponsors the night before, a black-tie gala in the Palazzo Brancaccio, and judging that awarded Best in Show to a one-off 16-cylinder 1932 Maserati V4 Sport Zagato, once owned by the personal physician of Pope Pius XII, returning to Rome for the first time in 90 years. Its owner, the retired New York fund manager Lawrence Auriana, keeps around 100 cars in Connecticut and flies a handful to events of this kind. What distinguishes the Rome event is its restriction to a single nationality of construction, across 16 classes. A second edition is confirmed for 1 to 4 April 2027.

The model has precedent. Lake Como's Villa d'Este held its first concours in 1929 and, after BMW's sponsorship at the turn of the millennium, has become the event by which the others are judged, fielding over 50 cars each May. Sir Michael Kadoorie, owner of The Peninsula Hotels, competes there and at Pebble Beach, and his Carmel property, The Quail, hosts what has arguably become the more culturally current gathering. This year's 6,000 all-inclusive Quail tickets sold out at GBP 1,170 a head, alongside six-figure commercial stands. The Peninsula Classics Best of the Best, invitation only since 2015, draws the Best in Show winners from Pebble Beach, Villa d'Este, The Quail, Amelia Island, Salon Prive, Hampton Court, Goodwood's Cartier Style et Luxe and the Palm Beach Cavallino Classic.

The economics are candid. William Heinecke, owner of Anantara's parent Minor Hotels, told Spear's he is not sure the return is quantifiable, given the scale of the investment, but that the event provides an experience and, not incidentally, introduces the brand to American collectors in a market where Anantara has no property. Owners cover transport: around GBP 8,000 to ship a car door to door from Los Angeles to Rome, or GBP 15,000 to GBP 18,000 to fly it, which most prefer. Hospitality at the Anantara starts from EUR 8,000 per couple or crew. Concours Croatia, held at the Boutique Hotel Alhambra on Losinj since 2024, runs 3 to 6 September at roughly half that.
articles.why: A principal entering a concours generates a logistics file, not a booking: shipping quotes, customs paperwork, insurance in transit, arrival windows and a car that must be presented immaculately at a set hour. This is concierge work of a high order.

briefs.b: Managing a smart house has moved from a rare skill to a standard requirement. In San Francisco, 83 per cent of household positions recruited in the past year required technical integration, with other cities following. New staff typically need 8 to 12 weeks to become comfortable with an unfamiliar household system.
briefs.src: Spear's, on the Morgan & Mallet Beyond the Butler 2025/26 report

briefs.b: At The Quail, the Peninsula-owned property near Carmel, last year's Best in Show was a track-restricted 1996 Ferrari F50 GT1 belonging to the Silicon Valley executive Art Zafiropoulo, who is reported to have turned down a USD 100 million offer for the car that day. The property has 93 guestrooms and was best known for its golf course until 2003.

Business jet manufacturers delivered 162 aircraft worldwide in the first quarter of 2026, almost 15 per cent more than a year earlier, with billings up 19 per cent to USD 6.1 billion. Embraer led the largest producers with deliveries up 26 per cent, and Pilatus nearly doubled PC-24 deliveries to nine. GAMA's second-quarter figures are due during the week of 24 August.
briefs.src: General Aviation Manufacturers Association (GAMA), quarterly shipments and billings

briefs.b: Average tenure across high-end household roles now sits at around three years, with nannies typically staying two to three, as staff become as mobile as the families they serve. Where the match is right, retention is markedly better: 92 per cent of personal assistants placed in Los Angeles by one agency stay beyond two years, as do the same proportion of nannies placed in Dubai.
briefs.src: Spear's, on the Morgan & Mallet Beyond the Butler 2025/26 report
